item.title: Cannibal Holocaust: The Movie That Made People Wonder If They Were Watching a Murder
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There are horror movies that scare you. There are horror movies that disgust you. There are horror movies that make you question the sanity of the people who made them.Then there is .Ruggero Deodato’s 1980 Italian exploitation film isn’t merely notorious because it contains graphic violence. Plenty of movies have blood, guts, torture, murder and other assorted reasons to lose your appetite. became infamous because it deliberately blurred the line between fiction and reality so effectively that people genuinely wondered whether they were watching an actual snuff film.Deodato wanted the movie to feel real.He succeeded so spectacularly that he ended up in court trying to prove that he hadn’t actually murdered his actors.That’s an impressive amount of trouble to get into over a movie.And just when you think the story can’t get any more disturbing, you discover that some of the animal deaths shown on screen were real.So yes, is one of the most messed-up movies ever made.But what makes it especially fascinating is that underneath all the gore, cannibalism, torture, exploitation and general cinematic depravity is an uncomfortable argument about the audience itself.The movie isn’t just asking, “How much violence can you handle?”Why do you want to watch it?It Starts With a Missing Film CrewThe premise is deceptively simple.A group of young American documentary filmmakers travels into the Amazon rainforest to make a documentary about supposedly primitive indigenous tribes.A rescue team eventually locates their abandoned film equipment. The reels are brought back to New York, where anthropologist Harold Monroe is asked to examine the footage and figure out what happened.This setup gives its most important structural trick.The movie switches between traditional narrative filmmaking and the supposedly recovered documentary footage.The footage becomes increasingly disturbing as Monroe watches it.At first, the filmmakers appear to be brave journalists documenting a dangerous environment.Then the truth becomes obvious.They deliberately provoke the people they’re filming. They manipulate situations. They stage events. They destroy property. They terrorize villagers. They treat human suffering as raw material for their documentary.They aren’t interested in understanding the people they’re filming.They’re interested in getting footage.And the uglier the footage becomes, the happier they are.That is the movie’s central idea.The documentary crew is willing to create suffering because they believe suffering makes good television.And that’s where Deodato starts turning the knife.Because the audience is watching the footage for exactly the same reason.The Found-Footage Trick Was Years Ahead of Its TimeModern audiences have become accustomed to shaky-camera horror. made found footage a mainstream phenomenon in 1999. later turned the technique into a major horror franchise.But was doing something similar in 1980.And it wasn’t merely using handheld cameras as a stylistic gimmick.Deodato wanted the footage to look like documentary material.The compositions are sometimes terrible.The filmmakers don’t always frame what they’re shooting properly.The footage looks unfinished.If the movie had looked like a traditional horror production, the audience could comfortably sit back and say, “It’s just a movie.”Deodato wanted to remove that safety net.He wanted viewers to wonder whether the people on screen were actually dying.Far better than anyone expected.People Actually Thought It Was RealThe movie’s reputation became so extreme that rumors spread that Deodato had made a genuine snuff film.The controversy was helped by a marketing strategy that encouraged the idea that the actors had actually disappeared.The actors had agreed not to appear publicly for a period following the film’s release.That made the rumors seem plausible.Then the Italian authorities got involved.“Mr. Deodato, we’re going to need you to come down to the police station.”“Because we think you murdered your cast.”Suddenly your low-budget cannibal movie has become a criminal investigation.Deodato eventually had to demonstrate that the deaths had been staged and that the supposedly murdered actors were still alive.The actors appeared in court, proving that the movie hadn’t actually been a snuff film.But Deodato had created such a convincing illusion that authorities had initially believed otherwise.That alone would make legendary.Unfortunately, the reality behind some of the film’s most notorious scenes is much less comfortable.This is the part where the movie’s “is it real?” controversy becomes genuinely unpleasant.The human deaths were fake.The animal deaths weren’t.Several animals were killed during production and their deaths were filmed.A turtle was butchered on camera.Other animals were also killed during production.The animal scenes weren’t special effects.They weren’t elaborate makeup effects.They were real animals being killed for the movie.That has become one of the most criticized aspects of the production, and understandably so.Even people who admire as an important piece of horror history have a difficult time defending those sequences.There’s a major difference between watching a fake human being hacked apart with a special-effects knife and watching an actual animal die.And that distinction makes some portions of considerably harder to watch today than they were when the movie first became notorious.The Movie Doesn’t Just Show ViolenceThis is another reason the movie remains so disturbing.The violence isn’t simply there because Deodato wanted to see how much blood he could put on screen.The movie repeatedly uses violence to demonstrate the documentary filmmakers’ moral collapse.They don’t merely record terrible events.They interfere with people’s lives.They manufacture situations.They behave like people who have discovered that the camera gives them permission to do things they wouldn’t otherwise do.That makes the filmmakers some of the most unpleasant protagonists in exploitation cinema.And they’re obsessed with getting footage.The movie essentially presents them as parasites feeding on human suffering.The audience is doing the same thing.And That’s Where Things Get Really CleverYou could argue that is a movie about exploitation made through exploitation.That’s what makes it so complicated.Deodato clearly had something to say about sensationalistic media.He was influenced by the way television news presented real violence to audiences, particularly the disturbing political violence that Italy had experienced.The movie’s fake documentary crew is basically a group of filmmakers who understand that shocking images sell.If they can make viewers uncomfortable enough, frightened enough or disgusted enough, they’ll keep watching.News organizations, television networks and eventually the internet have all learned that disturbing material attracts attention.The more outrageous the image, the more likely people are to stop scrolling.Deodato understood this decades before social media turned outrage into a business model.He was criticizing sensationalism while making one of the most sensationalistic movies imaginable.That’s either incredibly clever or spectacularly hypocritical.The Movie’s Most Uncomfortable QuestionThe most interesting question in isn’t whether the indigenous people are monsters.It’s whether the filmmakers are.And then it goes one step further.Are the filmmakers worse than the people watching them?That’s a nasty question to ask your audience.The movie knows exactly what you’re doing.You’re watching people suffer.You’re watching because it’s shocking.You’re waiting for the next horrible thing.The same impulse drives the fictional documentary crew.They want the next horrible thing too.They’re just willing to create it themselves.The difference between you and them, the movie suggests, is that they have a camera.That doesn’t exactly make for a comfortable viewing experience.The “Cannibals” Aren’t Really the PointThe title makes you expect a movie about cannibals.And sure enough, there are cannibalistic rituals and plenty of gruesome imagery.But the title is almost a distraction.The movie’s real subject is exploitation.The fictional documentary crew arrives expecting to find savages.Instead, they bring their own brand of savagery with them.They assume the people they’re filming are primitive.Meanwhile, the filmmakers themselves behave like violent animals.The movie deliberately reverses the audience’s expectations.The “civilized” outsiders become increasingly monstrous.The supposedly primitive locals become victims of people who believe their cameras make them superior.It’s a pretty bleak view of humanity.And it gets bleaker the longer the movie continues.Then There Is the Sexual ViolenceThis is where the film moves beyond ordinary gore and into territory that many viewers will simply find intolerable.annibal Holocaust contains scenes of sexual violence and sexual humiliation.They’re not presented in the relatively restrained manner that modern mainstream horror might use.Deodato’s exploitation-film approach means the material is deliberately confrontational.This is one of the reasons the movie remains difficult to recommend even to people who love extreme horror.There are movies where you can say, “It’s violent, but it’s fun.” isn’t really fun.It wants you to be uncomfortable.Sometimes it feels like the movie is actively daring you to keep watching.The Music Makes It Even StrangerOne of the movie’s strangest qualities is the contrast between the horrible images and Riz Ortolani’s score.The music isn’t constantly screaming at you that something terrible is happening.Some of it is surprisingly beautiful.That contrast makes certain sequences even more disturbing.A beautiful musical passage playing over horrifying images creates a bizarre emotional disconnect.You’re almost being encouraged to contemplate what you’re seeing rather than simply react to it.It’s one of the movie’s more effective techniques.The ugliness isn’t always accompanied by ugly music.Sometimes it’s accompanied by something hauntingly beautiful.That makes it feel less like a conventional horror movie and more like a particularly nasty piece of documentary footage.The Banned-Movie Reputation Made Everything WorseOnce began circulating internationally, its reputation grew.It became one of the notorious “video nasties” in Britain and was subject to censorship and bans in multiple countries.And naturally, that made people want to see it even more.There’s nothing quite like telling horror fans that something is forbidden.Suddenly everybody needs a copy.The movie became a forbidden object.People who had never heard of Ruggero Deodato suddenly knew the title.People who didn’t even like horror movies wanted to know what could possibly be so bad that governments were trying to stop people from watching it.The reputation became part of the experience.And once a movie develops that kind of mythology, it becomes almost impossible to separate the movie itself from the legend surrounding it.Does It Still Shock Today?But probably not always for the reasons it shocked audiences in 1980.Modern audiences have seen much more graphic special effects.Technology has made it possible to create incredibly realistic digital gore.We’ve also become accustomed to found footage.So the basic filmmaking tricks aren’t nearly as revolutionary as they once were.But still has something many modern extreme horror movies don’t.There is a nasty atmosphere surrounding the entire production.You know the controversy.You know the animals were really killed.You know the director was accused of making a snuff film.You know the actors had to prove they weren’t dead.And then you watch the movie.That knowledge changes the experience.You’re not just watching a fictional horror movie.You’re watching a movie with a history that is almost as bizarre as its fictional story.One of the Most Messed-Up Movies Ever MadeThere are plenty of movies that are more graphically violent than .There are movies with more gore.There are movies with more disturbing special effects.There are movies that are arguably more psychologically horrifying.But very few movies combine everything that makes so notorious.You have a fake documentary designed to look real.You have a director who was investigated because people thought the murders were genuine.You have actors who were deliberately hidden from the public.You have genuine animal deaths.You have extreme violence and sexual violence.You have a movie about exploitation that is itself deeply exploitative.You have a film that was banned and censored around the world.And underneath all of it is a question about why people consume violent images in the first place.That’s what makes more than just another gore movie.It’s an uncomfortable experiment.It wants to make you disgusted.It wants to make you suspicious.It wants to make you question the people holding the camera.And, eventually, it wants you to question yourself for still sitting there watching.That is a hell of a thing for a horror movie to accomplish.The strange thing is that isn’t necessarily a movie you’ll enjoy.Enjoyment almost feels like the wrong measurement.It’s more like an endurance test.You wonder what the hell you’re watching.You remind yourself that the human deaths are fake.Then you remember that some of the animal deaths aren’t.You start wondering how the hell this movie was ever released.Then you realize that somebody deliberately made it this way.And suddenly the movie becomes even more disturbing. isn’t the most technically impressive horror movie ever made.It isn’t the most entertaining.It certainly isn’t the easiest to recommend.But when the conversation turns to the most messed-up movies ever made, it belongs near the front of the line.Not because it has the most blood.Not because it has the most disgusting special effects.And not even because it has the most disturbing images.It belongs there because it crossed the line between movie and reality so effectively that people temporarily forgot they were watching fiction.And then there’s the truly uncomfortable part:Some of what they were watching really was real.That’s the legacy of .It’s a movie that tried to convince you that you were watching something you shouldn’t be watching.Forty-plus years later, it still succeeds.Just maybe not in the way anybody would want.It’s age restricted obviously so you have to be logged in, but they have it for free on Youtube

item.title: Troma Tuesday: Bloodsucking Freaks
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There are bad movies, there are terrible movies, and then there are movies like , a 1979 exploitation horror film that seems to have been created after someone asked, “What if we took every horrible idea we can think of and put them in one movie?”Also known as The Incredible Torture Show, the film follows Sardu, the owner of a theater where audiences believe they are watching elaborate stage performances. The problem is that the torture isn’t exactly acting.Sardu and his assistant Ralphus run a genuinely horrible little business, kidnapping people and subjecting them to increasingly ridiculous forms of torture while wealthy spectators watch and applaud.So basically, it’s dinner theater for people who should probably be investigated by the police.The movie wastes almost no time establishing that it has absolutely no interest in good taste. Sardu is played by Seamus O’Brien with the kind of theatrical enthusiasm usually reserved for children’s television villains, except this guy has a torture chamber instead of a magic castle.His victims are subjected to all sorts of increasingly absurd horrors, and the film presents much of it with a strange combination of exploitation-film sleaze and cheap stage-show comedy.That’s really the defining characteristic of .You aren’t supposed to take it seriously.The production values are extremely low, but that somehow becomes part of the entertainment. Sets look like they were assembled in somebody’s basement, the acting frequently resembles community theater performed by people who have just discovered horror movies, and the special effects range from surprisingly nasty to “someone just threw red paint on that.”And yet, somehow, it works.There is a bizarre energy running through the whole thing. The movie constantly seems to be daring the audience to keep watching.Just when you think you’ve reached the limit, it finds another way to make you wonder why you are still sitting there.The humor is incredibly dark and frequently offensive, which means this is definitely not a movie that has aged gracefully. A lot of the material is deliberately designed to provoke, and some of it is so tasteless that even exploitation-film veterans may find themselves staring at the screen wondering what exactly they just watched.But that’s also why the movie developed such a strong cult following. isn’t trying to be . It isn’t trying to be . It isn’t even particularly interested in being a conventional horror movie.It’s a midnight-movie experience.It’s occasionally hilarious.It’s frequently disgusting.And every once in a while, you catch yourself laughing at something that probably shouldn’t be funny.The biggest problem is that the movie’s relentless nastiness can become exhausting. There’s only so much torture, screaming and fake blood a viewer can absorb before the novelty begins to wear off.Still, if you enjoy bizarre exploitation cinema, is difficult to forget.It’s less a movie than a dare.Not remotely respectable.But if your idea of a good Friday night involves watching a completely unhinged late-1970s exploitation movie and repeatedly asking, “What the hell am I watching?”, delivers exactly what it promises.

item.title: Quoting Felix Rieseberg
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: The "old" version of Cowork runs model inference in the cloud, executing tool calls in an Anthropic-provided VM we shipped to your computer. We added the VM for capability, safety, and security reasons - mapping in just the data you explicitly added to your session. People loved what they were able to do with Claude but didn't love the disk, battery, and performance cost of running the VM locally. Also, people didn't love that closing your laptop means the work stops.The "new" version of Cowork runs model inference and the VM in the cloud. Each session gets its own sandbox, not sharing state with other sessions. When the VM needs something on the users' device (like a file), the desktop app is responsible for that file access tool call. [...]We think this solves a lot of problems we've heard about (like using Cowork from a phone, keeping work running, or getting all the same power without losing battery to the VM)

item.title: DOJ sued over ‘unprecedented’ 1,000 election monitors plan
item.author: 1axbnezgbzmewvzims5q6ccil8e099oygqqke7@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: The U.S. Supreme Court (SCOTUS) today threw out two pro-voter decisions in cases related to Washington’s legislative redistricting, sending them back to a lower court for new proceedings in light of the Court’s decision earlier this year in Louisiana v. Callais.That was the ruling that gutted the Voting Rights Act. Monday’s decision was the latest evidence that the landmark civil rights law is now essentially useless for stopping racial gerrymandering.A federal judge allowed the state’s new ban on using student IDs for voting to remain in place for this fall’s general election. But the judge also barred the state from enforcing a directive that prohibits state election officials from accepting a student ID as a valid form of identification to vote.That means: If a voter has no other way to prove their identity to vote, an election official can still consider a student ID as part of the evidence that he or she is qualified to vote.Still, the complexity and confusion could act as another barrier to voting for students, who already face more than their share of hurdles.A federal judge is set to rule on Trump’s effort to use vast amounts of Americans’ personal data to create state-by-state lists of people eligible to vote in federal elections, after being fully briefed on the legal arguments for and against Trump’s “State Citizenship Lists.”The decision is a victory for disability advocates who argued that the requirements increased the likelihood that valid ballots cast by those with difficulty getting to a physical polling place would be rejected on technicalities.In a Fox News interview, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito, one of Trump’s staunchest allies on the Court, rejected the growing chorus demanding reforms at the high court, saying the current justices are actually victims of intimidation. Alito said Democrats’ calls to expand the Court are a political attempt to influence the justices’ decisions.

item.title: The Atlanta Dream Can Poke And Prod You To Death
item.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
item.content:encoded: The argument against the Atlanta Dream says their transition-heavy style might be incompatible with playoff basketball. But in the three playoff games they’ve played so far, the latest a 92-82 home win over New York to open the second round, Karl Smesko's team has totally set the terms. As they see it, thisplayoff basketball: fast, tireless, always connected. Even when the Dream bump into issues running their halfcourt offense, they make the math work for them in other ways. The best offensive rebounder in league history wins them extra possessions, and a team defense that’s forced more turnovers than any other WNBA team this year sets up easy scoring opportunities against defenses on their heels. That made them a nightmare first-round matchup for the Washington Mystics, who turned the ball over more than any other WNBA team this year. Washington’s season indeed ended thanks to a 42-15 turnover differential across two games.Lest that stat be blamed on the young Mystics’ nerves, consider the 32 points Atlanta scored off 21 turnovers from veteran-stocked New York in Sunday's game. The fix for Game 2 on Wednesday sounds easy: Don’t turn the ball over. But the Atlanta Dream are a team designed to make it difficult. The Liberty’s problems weren’t all self-inflicted.

item.title: Phoebe Bridgers Showed Us How To See In The Dark
item.author: Kelsey McKinney
item.content:encoded: When the lights went out, a crisp, adolescent shriek rose from all sides of the arena, anticipating her arrival. But she did not come, not just yet. Instead, a silence fell heavy and unsettled where the shrieking had been, as if making space for the ball at the other end of the arena, descending ever so slowly, blinking blue, pulsing as if it were alive. More than 40,000 eyes fixated on the descending orb. It was round, but not a perfect sphere, with bumps and craters on its surface like a morning star weapon with all of its spikes truncated, or a children’s bumble ball powder coated in black. Though I was on the other side of the arena, and thousands of people were between me and the ball, it was dark, and there was nothing but air to separate us. I looked at the ball the way I look at the moon: with an awe bordering on reverence. Then it followed the same slow path back up into the rafters, and for a little while, I forgot about it. On the main stage a large half-circle dome rested atop the space where Phoebe Bridgers would eventually emerge, like the kind of mesh tents that protect food from the bites of prowling bugs. As the ball on one side of the arena disappeared, the tent on the other lit up. The shrieks began again. And then it lifted, lights gleaming from the edge of it straight down so that Bridgers' black dress was awash in so much light that it looked gray, and the whole dome had the appearance of a UFO lifting off the ground in a movie.

item.title: Turkish and Pakistani Troops to Saudi Arabia
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Hard to know quite what to make of this, or how much to make of it. But we’re getting what may be a preview of elements of a new era in the Middle East. According to a just released communiqué, Turkey and Pakistan will be sending troops to Saudi Arabia under the three countries’ new “Mecca Pact” to assist with fighting the Houthis in Yemen. The statement is very short on details. So it’s not clear whether this is a meaningful deployment of manpower and resources or something more nominal and symbolic. Nor is the timing of any deployment clear.

item.title: Jon Ossoff’s not-so-secret weapon against JD Vance and Marco Rubio
item.content:encoded: For more than a year, journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan had been trying — and largely failing — to raise awareness about the very strange story of Donald Trump and his aide Natalie Harp. Shortly after the 2024 election, the New York Times journalists published a profile of the lithe blonde in her early 30s, complete with photos of her gazing at Trump adoringly, explaining how she left him love letters with language like, “You are all that matters to me.” On Aug. 16, Haberman was still trying to raise the issue during an appearance on MS NOW, describing Harp as Trump’s “human binky.”But in the end, it was Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who woke up much of the public to this disturbing relationship by mentioning Harp on the campaign trail. “The defensive reaction from the White House was so over-the-top that it backfired, drawing more attention to the relationship. But a mystery remained. Haberman, Swan and many others had been talking about Harp, but it wasn’t until Ossoff said something that the White House truly lost their minds. The reaction likely had little to do with Ossoff’s comments, as elegantly as they were constructed. No, this recoil was more about the messenger than the message. At 39, Ossoff isn’t just young. He is strikingly handsome. The boyish good looks of his early career have matured into something closer to the old-fashioned allure of a 1960s-era movie star, such as Gregory Peck or Warren Beatty. Broad-chested, with great hair and a winning smile, Ossoff has a cool demeanor, good sense of humor and moral seriousness in a proportion that’s rare in politics — and that hasn’t really been seen since Barack Obama. Ossoff, in other words, can get it.Put another way, Ossoff is everything the 80-year-old president wishes he were, but isn’t. Harp’s presence is a touchy, daily reminder to both Trump and his staff of the president’s thick catalog failings as a human being. Having a young, handsome, talented man mock Trump for his emotional support aide had to have stung with a special precision. No one needs to tell the president or his staff that Ossoff feels just fine about himself — and doesn’t need a full-time emotional support aide to follow him around, praising his every move.Considering how much the White House communications staff is extremely online, they are also likely to know that Ossoff has become quite the thirst trap, even among young women and gay men who otherwise aren’t especially political on social media. As Grace Panetta of The 19th recently explained, the senator is a reliable, if unwitting, model for light-hearted crush content, much like what creators generate in tribute to movie stars like Timothée Chalamet or Tom Holland. “Take a scroll through Instagram and TikTok, and you’ll see fan edit-style videos of Ossoff Ossoff’s sex appeal doesn’t just offer a striking contrast with Trump’s oversized suits and comical combover. He’s also very different than men in the Republican ranks who are closer to his own age and, like himself, are widely seen as potential 2028 presidential candidates. At 42, Vice President JD Vance is also the subject a lot of online content. But most of it portrays him in a comically unflattering manner, with tiny dead eyes, oversized cheeks and a maniacal grin. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, 55, isn’t mocked for his looks, but he is often portrayed as a sad sack, a man too slow-witted and spineless to be much use beyond his role as Trump’s patsy. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, 46, is blessed with good looks that even three breakfast gin-and-tonics can’t take away. But with the help of Colin Jost on “Saturday Night Live,” he is mostly viewed like an overgrown frat boy crushing beer cans on his forehead. None come even close to the dreamboat treatment Ossoff receives. This disparate treatment is especially amusing because the MAGA movement has insisted for years that they are bringing back a more virile masculinity — supposedly to cure all the allegedly poisonous feminism inflicted upon America by those WNBA-loving Democrats. No doubt there are some people impressed by all the workout videos posted by MAGA leaders, though that audience probably doesn’t have much crossover with people who get second dates. But what all the chest-thumping and push-up contests of the right really communicates is overcompensation rather than reclaiming some “lost” masculinity.Beneath the right’s meltdown over Ossoff’s relatively tame comment about Harp was a molten layer of male insecurity. Steven Cheung, the volatile White House communications director, tweeted, “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics.” White House spokesman David Ingle called the senator a “cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid.” Both unwisely lobbed these insults from X accounts featuring photos of themselves. The handy comparison left the observer to contemplate how, with MAGA, it’s typically true that every accusation is itself a confession. Similarly, Trump compared Ossoff to Pee-wee Herman, a reference to a film that is older than the senator and only served to underscore how old and out of touch the president is. MAGA’s belief that masculinity is on the decline is more a reflection of their personal fears and resentments than an accurate picture of the world. Men who can just act normal continue to do fine, or as much as one can in this economy. As with many of the thirst-trap Democrats that are rising stars, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate hopeful Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a large part of Ossoff’s charm is that he possesses an easy masculinity, one comfortable with women’s equality. MAGA influencers may deny it, but men who actually like and respect women tend to be more attractive to women and gay men.Being chill with women’s power projects confidence. Insecure men are the ones who demand that women are forced into subservient roles, just so men can feel bigger. It speaks to an internal belief that they can’t win without cheating. That’s loser energy, not the Big Dictionary Energy being given off by Ossoff and this new crop of young, vigorous Democratic men.

item.title: San Francisco's best hotel cannot be killed
item.content:encoded: I am not a rock star, although I like to imagine myself as one. I imagine it so, so hard: packed stadiums, crowds numbering five figures going wild as I take my shirt off, shady managers hanging out backstage ready to ply me with Hefty bags full of pharmaceutical cocaine. But it’s too late for me, on the cusp of 50, to actually become a rock star — it certainly couldn’t be a skill or charisma issue, no sir — which is why there’s a tiny slice of the hospitality industry that exists to make patrons like me FEEL like rock stars, if only for a brief moment. This is where the legendary Phoenix Hotel, plopped down on Eddy Street right in the middle of San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, comes in.I have stayed at many hotels in San Francisco, but all of them were hotels. Elevator banks. Free continental breakfast. A sad gym on the third floor where one treadmill is always busted. You know the kind of hotel I mean. The Phoenix, which opened in the 1980s at the influence of legendary rock promoter Bill Graham, is not that kind of hotel. This was a place dreamed up to serve real-deal rock stars, and to make anyone else staying there feel like part of the greater entourage.Article continues below this adAnd until early this year, it was all set to die young, as so many of its more famous guests had, Kurt Cobain chief among them. Late in 2025, b. Patisserie co-owner Michel Suas was readying to take over the Phoenix’s lot and close down the hotel permanently, presumably using the land to build some kind of overpriced but good boulangerie. But at the last second, Suas had a change of heart! HONH HONH HONH! Enter local hotelier Binoy Patel, who took the reins of the property and is keeping the hotel open. That’s right, like a phoenix rising from the ashes. You read my mind to the letter.Given this fortuitous stay of execution, my SFGATE bosses thought that I should stay at the Phoenix during my annual “Drew comes to the Bay Area for a weekand eatsway too much” trip two months ago. As a Marylander, I was ignorant to the Phoenix’s charms before booking my room. It is now my favorite hotel in the city, and if new owner Patel messes with so much as a single AC outlet in the place, he and I will have words.I didn’t expect to love the Phoenix as much as I did, certainly not at first glance. No one stays in the Tenderloin for the Tenderloin. You stay in this part of town because you have some work engagement nearby. That’s why hotelier Chip Conley founded the hotel in the first place; it was close to venues where Graham booked gigs for headline acts. Otherwise, the place is located on a nondescript, run-down stretch of Eddy Street that’s a relative desert. The hotel itself is a refurbished roadside motel, the kind of place I’d normally expect to be murdered in. The only thing shielding your room door from the rest of the world is a red iron gate to the street next to the hotel office. So my first thought before ringing the front office door was, “This place better not suck.”Article continues below this adI was buzzed by a clerk who bore more than passing resemblance to Sweetums the Muppet: a bulky, tatted-up fellow with long scraggy hair and the beard to match. Sweetums could have been the bouncer at a Hells Angels bar if he wasn’t such a sweetheart. Instead, he manned the front desk at the Phoenix and warmly offered me a number of vital pointers. I needed to use my key card at the red gate anytime I came or went, there was always free coffee in the front office if I needed it, and logging onto the hotel’s Wi-Fi required him to perform a live demo for me.“I can’t do it the usual way?” I asked Sweetums.“Doing it the usual way here is s—t,” he told me. But doing it his way worked like a charm.Article continues below this adI walked into a concrete courtyard loosely festooned with palm trees, potted succulents, and basket chairs surrounding a fat round pool. An outdoor performance stage loomed toward the back. No one was swimming in the pool when I first entered the courtyard; the water was populated exclusively by aging pool noodles, some of which had bite marks in them. But the water looked clean, which is more than you can say for the average Motel 6 pool. I crossed the courtyard to the outdoor staircase leading up to my second floor room. Standing sentry by the staircase was a huge, colorfully tiled sculpture of a frog playing the guitar. Your mother would describe this hotel as “kind of funky,” and she’d be correct.But the ultimate test for this kind of novelty hotel is your room itself. You want a hotel that’s only seedy. I’ve stayed at actual seedy hotels … the kind of hotels where s—t doesn’t work. They are not charming. So my room at the Phoenix would determine which side of the line the hotel fell on.Article continues below this adIf you’ve read this far, you won’t be surprised to learn that my room was perfect. One side of it was dominated by a floor-to-ceiling window looking out onto the courtyard, just in case any other guests wanted to watch me and a groupie going at it. Seeing as how I’ve been faithfully married for 24 years, the chances of me indulging in that particular rock star fantasy were minimal. But it was nice to know I had the option if I so chose.As for the room itself, it had everything I would have wanted from a mainstream hotel room. The bed was comfy. There were multiple charging outlets available to me, many hidden inside of retro furnishings that scanned like film props. And I didn’t need a tutorial from Sweetums on how to operate the shower or the light switches. My only beef was that the soft neon lamp hanging over my bed didn’t work, but I probably wouldn’t have used it for longer than two minutes anyway.This was a goodass hotel room, and it served as a perfect base of operations for me as I spent all week covering assignments in North Beach, Cow Hollow, Marin, Palo Alto, and elsewhere. Anytime I was slogging through my day of field reporting, I knew that my plush room at the Phoenix would be waiting for me. Best of all, when I asked Sweetums if there were any good places for breakfast nearby, he immediately told me to hit Brenda’s French Soul Food, another local institution I had been heretofore unaware of. I went to Brenda’s the following morning and ordered the bananas foster French toast, plus a breakfast sandwich. You know, for balance. I ate so well that brunch, I needed to burn some serious calories afterward.Article continues below this adAnd where better to do that than in the Phoenix pool?This was August, mind you. Temperatures in San Francisco that time of year aren’t always conducive to pool days, so I suited up with the mercury hovering around a crisp 65 in the hotel’s courtyard. I fully expected the water to be even colder than that, so imagine my surprise when I jumped off the edge and KERSPLOOSH! Suddenly I was warmer and happier than I’d been all trip. The Phoenix pool isn’t so hot as to feel gross, it’s just well calibrated for a warm swim in a city that wants you to slowly freeze to death. Once in the pool, I knew immediately that leaving the pool would render me a pile of chattering teeth. So I grabbed one of the chewed-up pool noodles and lounged to my big fat heart’s content.Article continues below this adI felt no danger from the dirty street outside, nor did I feel embarrassed to be a 49-year-old man, rash guard and all, swimming all by himself in the middle of a random weekday. I know that Sweetums was standing sentry at the front desk, and I knew that I was exactly where I wanted to be: kicking back in the heart of one of the best cities in the world, with not a single worry on my mind. If that’s not the life of a rock star, I don’t know what is.

item.title: Patience Is Paying Off For Bryce Young
item.author: Israel Daramola
item.content:encoded: I'm not sure when we fell into the collective delusion that first-round quarterbacks should be capable of leading an NFL team on Day 1. Was it induced by the take economy? Is this sports radio's fault? Did Joe Burrow's early success create this standard? I can understand certain teams like the Browns or Jets believing it necessary to have their top draft pick run the offense right away, because they have little hope otherwise, but what's everyone else's excuse? While you may get Andrew Luck or Lamar Jackson on occasion, often these teams just end up stunting the growth of potential stars, who end up having to rehab their careers and abilities elsewhere.I was thinking about these things Sunday night while watching Bryce Young have arguably the best game of his career for the Carolina Panthers, against the Detroit Lions. Young led the Panthers to a 32-26 win while throwing for 329 yards and two touchdowns on 29-of-41 passing. Second-year wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan was the biggest beneficiary, accounting for 43 percent of the Panthers' total yardage. He caught 14 passes for 192 yards, and accounted for those two TD passes.Young and McMillan's chemistry has been building since last season, and never was it more useful than when last night's game was on the line. Despite outplaying the Lions for most of the game, the Panthers were in a spot of trouble late in the fourth quarter. After Detroit scored and cut the lead to six, Young and the offense took over on their own 36-yard line with 3:38 left to play. At the very least, the Panthers needed to get a first down and force a few timeouts out of the Lions. A one-yard run by Chuba Hubbard forced the first burned timeout, and then a penalty followed by an incompletion put Young in a tough spot. Suddenly it was third-and-14, only 22 seconds had come off the clock, and Young was scrambling to avoid pressure. That's when he saw McMillan near the sideline, and made an absurd throw to invite an incredible catch:

item.title: The Case Against Exceptionalism
item.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
item.content:encoded: The first line in a Min Jin Lee novel gives you the whole story. In Free Food For Millionaires, it’s “Competence can be a curse.” In her follow-up, , it’s “History has failed us, but no matter.” Both establish the thesis and themes of the novels, and of her larger project of writing about the Korean diasporic experience. The first line of Lee’s latest novel, , does the same: “The rules of engagement have changed already.” The novel, which came out last week nearly a decade after was published, situates her characters—and by extension, the Korean diaspora—at a point of transition where they must adapt. Ever concerned with the financial realities of Korean families, in , Lee considers the cost, both economic and human, of a people striving to elevate itself. tells the story of a community centered around a hagwon founded in Los Angeles by Korean immigrants. Hagwons are cram schools that are incredibly popular in South Korea, and in the U.S. among Korean communities. They exist to supplement the day-to-day education students get at school. Students often attend them every day after school and late into the night, doing extra work to get ahead academically and to prepare for the highly competitive exams required for admission to the top Korean universities, as well as elite American universities.

item.title: O Superman, Laurie Anderson
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: O Superman by artist Laurie Anderson from 1981. Some of the lyrics:‘Cause when love is goneThere’s always justiceThere’s always forceThere’s always MomSo hold me, MomIn your long armsIn your long armsYour electronic armsSo hold me, MomYour petrochemical armsIn your electronic armsThis is a song about how basically technology cannot save you. It’s about a lot of things: justice, safety, power.As a kid growing up in rural Wisconsin, this kind of music wasn’t available to me, so I only actually heard this for the first time fairly recently. So I thought I’d post it in case you hadn’t really heard it either — that and the message & meaning it carries is relevant these days.

item.title: Memories of the Hastert Years … and the Ironies of History
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: It’s hard to know what to say about former Republican Speaker of the House Denny Hastert, whose death at the age of 84 was reported this morning. Few if any political leaders in modern American history have experienced a fall quite so ignominious and total. The obvious point of comparison is Richard Nixon. But post-Watergate Nixon was never without his defenders and supporters. All but his most adamant critics granted significant successes of his presidency. And by the time of his death in 1994, he’d made significant progress in being treated by many as a sage elder statesman, albeit a greatly tarnished one. Hastert remains almost a test case of a top political leader whose fall was immediate and absolute. He came as close as one can come to have to having zero public defenders (though a significant number of former colleagues wrote leniency letters on his behalf at sentencing in 2016). What stands out in my mind are two moments, one from his moment of ascent to power and another at the denouement but certainly not the nadir of career. Go back to 1998. The so-called Lewinsky scandal had been trundling forward for most of the year. Republicans are giddy about the Red Tsunami that was about to supercharge the existing GOP majority. Predictions of a 30- or 40-seat pick up were common and assumed. (I was one of few people I knew to basically predict no wave at all; it was simply a matter of watching the polls rather than the bipartisan hype.) When Democrats ended up gaining five seats, House Speaker New Gingrich was summarily tossed overboard — a mix of the failure of his wild overpromising and slowly building frustrations with his erratic and high drama leadership style.

item.title: Atlanta’s Least Heralded Relievers Did The Most
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The Atlanta Braves are not the best team in this postseason, but there do seem to be more of them than anyone else. Manager Walt Weiss has appeared blithely unconcerned by the math that demonstrates that the more pitching changes a team makes, the greater the likelihood that some of them will turn to shit.And yet Weiss persists, because these are the tools that have been provided for him. After the attrition of the regular season, he has at his disposal three discernible starting pitchers; the best of those, Chris Sale, already had to close out one game against the Phillies in Atlanta's wild-card win, and has not yet started in the team's NLDS. In a more normal environment, this "all hands on deck" strategy would be pointing toward a very predictable outcome: a mutiny by the crew.But Sunday was the acme of that plan to date. The Braves beat the Dodgers, 3-2, in Game 2 of the National League Division Series, because of stellar work by a 32-year-old ultra-journeyman whose career has been dominated by surgery rehab, and a 21-year-old puppy who fetches whatever is thrown his way because that's what 21-year-olds get to do this time of year. More or less everyone in the Atlanta bullpen was called upon to contribute to the team's most important game of the year so far, and more or less everyone did.

item.title: How Lucy Yu Learned To Ask For Help
item.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
item.content:encoded: Who among us has not floated the idea of starting a bookstore to our friends and partners, as a way out of the nightmare that is 9-to-5 work and LinkedIn hell? In 2021, Lucy Yu actually did it. She had been unhappily working as a chemical engineer and socking away money, and when she had $40,000 saved, she took the plunge and opened Yu & Me Books, the first Asian American woman-owned bookstore in New York City.Yu & Me Books was the fantasy embodied. It was a cozy space in Chinatown, filled with Yu's favorite books and new releases, and she hosted author and community events each week. But that fantasy was only possible because Lucy was pushing her body and mind to the absolute limit of what she could handle. Everything changed when a fire nearly destroyed her shop in 2023. I've been a fan and supporter of Yu & Me since it first opened, but I was curious to talk with Lucy about how the fire forced her to learn that in order to take care of her community, she had to learn to take care of herself first. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RCSOXHeHX-4

item.title: With Four Weeks to Go, Dems Are in the Driver’s Seat
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: With voting coming to a close four weeks from tomorrow, Morning Memo will be shifting its focus to the midterms, with dual track coverage of the horse race and the outsized expectations for Democrats as an opposition party, if they win.Usually at this point in the election cycle, expectations management is focused on not being so confident that it dampens your voters’ sense of urgency to get to the polls, mutes the post-election news coverage of your victory, and takes the edge off the mandate you win.But this cycle Democrats are saddled with enormously unrealistic expectations about what they can and should do the election. Even if they win both chambers of Congress, Democrats even in normal times would face structural, institutional, and political limitations that are very real and will make achieving quick, tangible, meaningful reform virtually impossible.But these are not normal times.President Trump has done astonishing damage across all of civic life, in the public and private sectors. He will continue to enjoy the strategic and tactical advantage that comes when you don’t care about collateral damage and when wanton destruction is easier than building enduring institutions.In addition, many of the ingredients that gave rise to the Trump era remain: a degraded information ecosystem, a fierce right-wing propaganda machine, a nihilistic Republican Party not committed to democracy or to a robust civic life, among many others.That doesn’t mean the election is not important or that an opposition party can serve no function — but it’s obvious that Democrats will come in shouldering the weight of pressure to move fast and decisively in a system that favors neither. The opposition will also face the unhelpful dichotomy that while the American political system has slid over the edge toward neo-fascism, most of the political press still covers campaigns and elections with the same dated tropes and stale constructs — as if things haven’t fundamentally changed.It can’t be the case that whether we get democracy or fascism, the rule of law or authoritarianism, reform or systemic corruption rides on the result of each election. Yet, here we are.Midterm Elections Watch: Senate Edition: The Senate Leadership Fund — the super PAC aligned with the Senate GOP — has paused funding in the North Carolina Senate race and plans to invest $14 million to save Sen. Roger Marshall (R) in Kansas.: Ken Paxton’s estranged wife can’t bring herself to say his name, but in a new ad urges Republicans to vote for the GOP ticket: “Let’s talk about the elephant in the room. In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team. It’s about getting the whole team across the finish line.”Midterm Elections Watch: House EditionDemocratic Congressional Campaign Committee political director Brooke Butler predicts Democrats will carry the House with as many as 240 seats. Democrats have held a House majority that large only once in the last three decades: the high-water mark of 257 seats after the 2008 election.If Republicans lose the House, Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) is likely to run for House minority leader, Punchbowl reports: “Jordan won’t admit it publicly, but his inner circle of aides, advisers and friends is plotting for a leadership election, and he’s discussed it with people close to him.”Midterm Election Shenanigans WatchThe George Election Board’s request for the Trump DOJ to intervene in the state’s voting systems was a rogue act by the board’s executive director, the board chair told Votebeat. More here.Reuters: How Trump’s obsession with ‘rigged’ voting machines spread across US governmentContrary to earlier reports, election denier Kurt Olsen is still employed at the Justice Department, according to the Washington Post. The newspaper had previously reported that Olsen resigned not just as head of the “grand conspiracy” investigation in south Florida, but from DOJ entirely:A message Olsen sent Monday announcing his departure was originally misinterpreted by officials in Washington and Miami as a full resignation from the Justice Department, but Olsen later clarified to his bosses that he still intended to remain a department employee, even though he is no longer attached to the case, one of those people said Wednesday. His current assignment remains unclear.Shock! Trump Behind Pro-Trump Govt AdsPresident Trump was directly involved in ordering the use of $20 million in DHS funds to air TV ads in the stretch run of the midterm elections extolling his presidency, the NYT reports:Mr. Trump was eager to see the laudatory ads on the air and told Russell T. Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, to come up with the money from within the government, the people said. Mark Paoletta, the budget office’s counsel, and Will Scharf, the White House counsel, both said it would be legal to use D.H.S. funds. The president and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, both spoke with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, about the ads.“My party is being infiltrated by people like Bo French. Nick Fuentes goes to Dallas and meets with a bunch of Republican leaders. This guy is a Nazi. We’ve got all these people getting on their little podcasts and so forth, saying: ‘We’re just asking questions about the Jews.’”—TPM’s Christopher Mathias: Chris Rufo — Known For ‘DEI’ and ‘CRT’ Panics — Tries to Make ‘the Indian Question’ a ThingJudge Blocks Border Wall In Big BendA federal judge in El Paso on Friday temporarily blocked construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including the eponymous national park.: Marimar Martínez, the woman shot five times by a Border Patrol agent during Operation Midway Blitz, is expected to file a federal lawsuit today “that includes new ballistics analysis and video animation showing the agent was not in harm’s way when he opened fire,” the Chicago Tribune reports.: DHS agents not only tracked and intimidated people observing ICE activity during Operation Catch of the Day, but allegedly stored information about them in a Palantir-built database, according to newly unsealed court filings reviewed by Wired.: A Hasidic Jew who protested against the Israeli flag may now be deported, the New York Times reports.US Rushes Bombers Home From UKNYT: “The United States rushed over the weekend to withdraw all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from an air base in southern England after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the installation, two U.S. officials said on Sunday.”Dennis Hastert, 1942-2026The longest-serving Republican speaker of the House — who turned out to be, in the words of his sentencing judge, a “serial child molester” — died of natural causes at his Illinois home over the weekend at age 84.Dennis Hastert served in Congress for 20 years, eight of them as speaker. But it wasn’t until 2015, eight years after he left office, that his abuse decades earlier of wrestlers while he was a wrestling coach emerged. Hastert pleaded guilty to illegally structuring payments to one of his victims and served 13 months in prison.It remains one of the mysteries of American politics that the Denny Hastert saga — a tragic coda to the corruption of the Tom Delay era — never broke through into the wider political consciousness.

item.title: Jaguars Junction: Week 4
item.author: Hamilton Nolan
item.content:encoded: Are you grasping for an explanation of the Jacksonville Jaguars' typically excellent performance? Look no further than the Microsoft Surface. Microsoft Surface tablets are in the hands of all the Jaguars coaches on the sidelines now, and players are allowed to look at them as well. You can even buy a Jacksonville Jaguars skin to customize your own Microsoft Surface at home. With Microsoft Surface, the opposing team can no longer hide behind their helmets. A few clicks or swipes of the virtual keyboard brings up all the information about them that was heretofore concealed. That includes photographs of the faces of each player, their height, weight, and colleges attended. Where past generations of football teams may have focused on developing better footballs or shoulder pads, the Microsoft Surface delivers the Jacksonville Jaguars the most powerful differentiator in the modern NFL: information. Data unearthed by Microsoft Surface can be relayed by coaches directly into earpieces in the helmets of each Jacksonville Jaguar. Then a defensive lineman, for example, can look across at the offensive lineman on the other team and say, "Your facemask no longer intimidates me. You are Dalton Risner. You attended Kansas State University. Your favorite food is chocolate. I can tell you the exact address of your parents and other loved ones. A team of assassins is sitting outside of their homes, as we speak. The choice before you now is simple. Either you allow me to run past you, or you will never see them again." Then the Jaguars player could describe in detail what their houses look like on Google Maps. Dalton Risner doesn't know if the other guy is telling the truth, or if the assistant coach just fed him all that information from the sidelines. But does he want to take the chance?

item.title: No human is illegal
item.content:encoded: One patch I kept seeing over and over again is…No human is illegal on stolen land.I get it. It’s supposed to point out the hypocrisy of complaining about illegal immigration in a country that was founded by stealing it from and genociding the people who already lived here.But it also kind of implies that if we done that—if we’d found an empty continent just waiting to be settled—it would be OK to keep some people out.No human is illegal. Period.

item.title: Three giraffes
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: "I took this in 2025 in the Maasai Mara, Kenya, in the Oltepesi area. Three young giraffes were standing side by side on the savanna and looked back at me with great curiosity. Right behind the middle one stood a single umbrella acacia, perfectly lined up with its head and neck. The giraffe seemed to be wearing the tree, like a green hairdo or a fancy hat. Nothing was staged or arranged; it was a matter of being in the right spot at the right moment’"Photograph: Dirk Koster/Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards 2026Via The Guardian, where this was one of several featured photos from the Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards finalists for 2026. (Image cropped for emphasis from the original)

item.title: "Send me a man who reads!" (International Paper advertisements of the 1960s)
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: These advertisements from International Paper ran in a variety of magazines in the early 1960s. I encountered them in , which our family subscribed to because it was the cheapest magazine subscription available via my high school's subscription-selling annual fund drive. I clipped these ads out, posted them in various places, and saved them for decades until they disappeared during one of my moves between apartments as a young adult.As an adult I've wanted to see the ads again because they were so influential on my high-school brain. Some years ago I wrote to International Paper asking if any copies, prints, posters etc were available, but received no reply. My current neighborhood library for understandable reasons does not keep hard copies of decades-old magazines. I found these two in a 2013 post at Reactor Fire.

item.title: What the fuck is this?
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich

item.content:encoded: UPDATE: 11:33 EDT: it has come to my attention that the image of Piss-Drunk Pete at the top of this post was generated by a six-fingered plagiarism robot and is NOT REAL. This is why I should never write a post when I’m sleep-deprived. Sorry, everyone. I will vow to do better. I still stand behind the other 99% of this post. —Jeff T.I am now back at home, after having spent four awesome days visiting Daughter Katie and Son-in-Law Norrin. It’s always wonderful to hang out with them both, and we all had a great weekend.This morning, after a long night of air travel, I’m once again rather burned out and in need of a day to recover — so please forgive me for posting a couple of quick hits. I’ll be back tomorrow with the usual full-length screed. Thank you for your attention to this matter.Bribe the Vote™ — Preznit Fuckwit’s patently illegal scheme to line the pockets anyone who’ll vote for Republicans — rolls on. But his latest ruse is a bit different. This time, he’s giving free money to every , no strings attached. Just remember who did you a solid, when it comes time to pull the lever.“I’m pleased to announce that over— twenty million seniors on Medicare will soon be receiving a— deposit of nearly one hundred dollars directly into— THEIR bank accounts. Through our— war on fraud, we have already reduced your— Medicare premiums by— $132 per year, which is a record. Now, October premiums will be offset— with these additional funds, and seniors will be— able to use that money— for their healthcare needs.”Okay, let’s leave aside the fact that Dear Demented Leader is so goddamned illiterate that he can barely read off the cue cards his minders put in front of him, resulting in that weird, halting cadence of his. Let’s talk instead about what he’s doing here.Look, I’m an and on Medicare. Sure, I’ll take the money. Why not? Who wouldn’t like a ? But let’s be clear about two things. He’s doing it through slight of hand, by robbing Peter to pay Paul, as the saying goes — and even Congressional Republicans think that Donny’s financial hocus-pocus A Republican congressional aide told Dan Diamond of the Washington Post that lawmakers had been planning to use the fund to help fund several health programs this year, and were taken aback by Trump’s announcement.Second, ‘almost a hundred’ is nice, for sure, but it’s a drop in the bucket in Donny’s inflationary hellscape. I hope Dear Leader doesn’t imagine that his almost-a-hundred is going to be a life-altering event for anyone.Donny wants a cookie for doling out a tiny pittance to you, while at the same time grifting billions off his gullible worshipers. He’s too dim to realize that Fox News is doing him a favor by not airing any of his batshit speeches. Donny’s toxic right now. He’s fucking kryptonite. Boo fucking hoo, dipshit. Maybe try not to Now what. The fuck. Is this?On the left is our piss-drunk, power-mad, in-love-with-himself Secretary of Death, Pete Kegstand, a couple-three days ago.On the right is some fucking asshole.How does this keep happening? Why does it seem as if these fucksnoots are trying to create their own Turd Reich?Why does the administration’s iconography look as if it were deliberately copied from a 1930 Nuremberg rally?Why does the Pocket Nazi, Obergruppenführer Greg Bovino, dress as if he were literally a Nazi in your pocket?Why does Stephen Miller always look like he’s trying to win a Joseph Goebbels look-alike contest?How is it that the Space Nazi sieg-heils in exactly the same manner — — as that fucking asshole used to?Spoiler alert: This is not an accident. It’s not some weird coincidence.These fascist shit-kazoos are not just Nazi wanna-bees. They’re literal Nazis, They’re the baddies, and they Lastly, please indulge me for a moment, and allow me to be a proud father.Twenty years ago, at the age of fifteen, Daughter Katie started a weekly webcomic about video gaming. She called it Awkward Zombie. She’s still at it. This morning, Katie posted her . I think that’s a pretty fucking cool accomplishment.And now, it’s Daily Claudia time.Today, I want to celebrate Ms Spouse’s friendship with her bestie Kathy, because I love revisiting just how much these two genuinely enjoyed each other’s company.This next one is outside the Ossining restaurant 3 Westerly Bar and Grill, on July 29, 2021. I’m so fond of it that it’s been the desktop image on my laptop since the day I took it.This last one is also from 3 Westerly, on August 28, 2025. I know I’ve posted it before, but come on — how fucking awesome is it?Have a great Monday, everyone. Yes, I know — I ended up writing a full-length post. I didn’t intend to. Shut up.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: The Valkyries Are Fighting Firepower With Frenzy
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: Before Sunday's semifinal Game 1 in Ballhalla, the Valkyries threw a little ceremony to honor Janelle Salaün for winning Sixth Player of the Year. Salaün's unanimous approval by voters is one indication of her team's tremendous depth; another, stronger one is that the Valkyries overwhelmed the Aces, 71-60, thanks primarily to their bench and even as Salaün missed both of her shots, scored two points, and played six anonymous minutes.What makes the Valkyries special? Simply: There are so many of them. Sure, fine, also the defense, though the Valks' defense is in large part a function of their depth. Their bench scores more than anyone else's, and no other playoff team's starters get anywhere near as much rest as Golden State's. Not having to manage around the limits of, say, Breanna Stewart playing 33 minutes per game allows Natalie Nakase's team to operate at a higher intensity for a longer amount of time and mix up the looks they give opponents. However, the unfortunate predicament facing any team structured to play this way is that the playoffs are all about playing Breanna Stewart as much as possible, not having a bunch of overtalented eighth players buzzing around off the bench.At least in theory. Game 1 showed how devastating Golden State's depth can be. You could see it in the way the Valkyries closed, with Kaitlyn Chen not only stepping in for Veronica Burton but running a form of crunch-time offense built around her repeatedly cooking Mai Yamamoto. You could see it in Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young's combined 9-for-29 night, the product of being hounded for every inch of court by a rotating cast of good athletes. You could see it personified in Aminata Gueye, a backup center the team signed two weeks ago and trusted to play her first non-garbage time minutes in a crucial playoff game against the best player in the league. You could definitely see it in the gaudiest stat of the night: the Valkyries' 17 offensive boards and plus-27 rebounding margin. That was the subject of the first question Nakase fielded in her postgame presser, and she credited the rebounding masterclass to the team's depth.

item.title: Eagles Fans Demonstrate How To Get Humbled By Opposing Coaches
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: I want you to imagine you are a Philadelphia Eagles fan. I know it can be difficult to formulate a theory of mind for them, but if it can be done for a bat, it can be done for a Philadelphian. OK, ready? Go.You are a Philadelphia Eagles fan. You suddenly have a constant craving for large sandwiches. Your head is now filled with detailed biographical knowledge of several local meteorologists. Every proper noun in this story is familiar. "Pond Lehocky" means something to you. The shouted phrase "FORMAN MILLS" plays randomly in your head at all hours. You are drunk. Drunker than normal, because it is game day. You have probably been tailgating, which is so important to you that you have reinvented collective bargaining from first principles in order to protect your right to drink next to the stadium as opposed to one lot farther out.You are drunk and feeling good. Your Eagles have been leading since the first drive of the second quarter. They are up 20-10 on the Rams. But not all is well. Jalen Hurts completes just two passes in the second half. They run an unsuccessful Tush Push. They unadvisedly go for it on fourth down with about eight minutes left, and fail, then allow Los Angeles to score touchdowns on two quick drives. The Eagles lose.

item.title: Jackson Chourio Was Nails
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: Mason Miller wasn't looking like himself by the time Jackson Chourio stepped to the plate in the bottom of the ninth of Game 2 of the NLDS. After making quick work of three Brewers hitters in the bottom of the eighth inning, Miller was trusted to go back out there for the ninth and protect the Padres' 3-2 lead. It was only the third time all season he'd been called on to pitch six outs, and by the time he'd recorded two outs in the ninth he'd also issued three walks. The most unhittable pitcher in baseball wasn't getting hit, but he was in trouble nonetheless.None of this is meant to diminish what Chourio did next. It is only meant to establish that baseball is a game that unfolds as a series of discrete moments that are not necessarily related to what came before. The first three batters Miller faced were blown away, and then three more benefited from the fact that he was having some trouble locating his slider. Chourio watched all of this from the dugout and the on-deck circle, and as he stepped to the plate with two outs and the bases loaded and his team down a run, he had to decide how to attack Miller. Baseball's most indomitable relief pitcher had just given out three free passes, and it's very rare that anything nearly as good as getting on base comes from swinging at one of Miller's pitches. A good time to keep the bat the shoulder, no?Miller, too, had to make a decision. He could decide to let what had already happened in the inning affect how he approached Chourio's at-bat, or he could put it all out of his mind. He could remember that he's Mason fucking Miller, the guy who struck out 129 batters in 70 regular-season innings and allowed 13 earned runs all year. He could decide that everything that had just happened didn't matter, and all he needed to do to get his team a win was get one out.

item.title: Being the Queen Can Be Miserable
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Disney movies make little girls want to grow up to be a princess. They have beautiful dresses, loyal servants, a magical fairy godmother, and they end up marrying the prince of her dreams. But then what? Eventually you'll be a queen, and the lives of real queens were anything but fun. In real life as a queen, you didn't get to choose who you marry, possibly a prince or king who may be quite inbred, and you might not even speak the same language. Then your duty was to bear children of royal blood. Plenty of people wanted to kill your spouse or children or even you, and the rest of them wanted something from you. Meanwhile, you had to keep up the decorum expected from royalty. Your subjects might not even like you. It was a lifelong sentence of no privacy or agency.
