item.title: This time, take Trump literally
item.author: 1axchqbo0ons8c114rd9dx657actsnmxj6kctf@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Earlier this year, The New York Times asked Donald Trump whether he regretted not ordering the National Guard to seize voting machines in swing states after the 2020 election. His answer was chilling: "Well, I should have."Trump is telling us what he plans to do in this year's midterms. He is trying to rig the elections and subvert their results. While we have been able to stop him so far, there is no guarantee that we will continue to prevail in the weeks ahead.Yet despite the obvious signs of Trump's plan, too many reporters and pundits downplay it. They adhere to the false neutrality that has come to dominate legacy media coverage over the last decade.No phrase captures this attitude more clearly than the admonition to take Trump seriously but not literally. The suggestion is that only out-of-touch elites pay attention to his actual words. Real voters — and those in the media who claim to speak for them — know to focus on his vibes.When it comes to voting and elections, this advice has been catastrophically wrong. In 2020, Trump's words before the election were prophetic about what he would do afterward. His refusal to concede foreshadowed the attack on Jan. 6, 2021.Trump is once again in power, and he is again telling us his plan. He has weaponized the entire federal government — including the Department of Justice and the U.S. Postal Service — to make voting more difficult.He is threatening to deploy federal agents at the polls and to disrupt voting. And he is reaching for every other tool of election rigging: partisan gerrymandering, restrictions on voter registration, attacks on mail-in voting and the use of bogus lists to purge eligible citizens from the rolls.But most dangerous is what he has been saying for more than a year about the counting, tabulation and certification of election results. Despite what the U.S. Constitution says, he has repeatedly claimed the power to direct this process.This is not a new idea. It has been his plan all along.

item.title: Midori Hirano (Interview)
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Midori Hirano, a Japanese composer and pianist based in Berlin. The last time we recommended her music was in 2021. She uses synth and piano to create electroacoustic pieces that reflect her classical training as well as interest in more experimental compositional techniques. Her latest record is a new score for , the 1990 film by Nietzchka Keene set in Iceland and starring Björk. Reflecting on the process of making the score, she told us, “I think this film has a lot of ambiguity showing different kinds of emotions and you can’t really define who is good or bad actually. And I think that electronic sounds are well suited to expressing subtle aspects of human psychology, while an acoustic instrument like the piano, the nature of the instrument can be quite strong, so I feel it can sometimes limit the kind of impression or feeling it creates.” We’re also revisiting her 2020 record, , whose piano pieces are complex and processed through a range of effects. A conversation with Midori follows the streaming links.What’s your earliest memory of music?When I was growing up in Japan in the ‘80s, it was still the bubble era, and there were many children around me who were taking piano lessons.So whenever I went to play at neighbor’s house, I often heard someone playing the piano. But at the same time, my grandparents bought my brother and me a Super Famicom, which had just been released back then. I often played games like Super Mario with my brother and friends, and the music from those games gradually became embedded in my memory, without me even realizing it. So when I think back on it, both the sound of the piano and the sounds of video games are equally part of my earliest musical memories.How did you get started with piano? What was the first piece that you learned that felt like a real accomplishment?As I mentioned above, so many children around me were taking piano lessons when I was a child, so I just became interested in playing it as well. Even in my small hometown, there seemed to be someone giving piano lessons on almost every block in my neighbourhood at that time. But before I started playing piano when I was around six, we had a small pump organ at home, and I remember just playing around on it, making whatever sound I felt like.I don’t really remember what the first piece I managed to play properly was, but I think it was probably one of those standard little pieces by Bach or Mozart.What were the artists/albums that early on helped point you in the direction of your own sound?When I started making electronic music in early 2000s, glitch and all kinds of experimental electronic music were thriving at the time. So I’m sure I was inspired by a lot of those music. But if I had to pick just one, it would have to be Tujiko Noriko’s , which was released on Mego. I found it very refreshing how freely field recordings, sampled sounds, and noise were arranged, yet somehow they all came together well as a pop song. is an interesting blend of synth and piano. How do you think about using either instrument – does a musical idea occur to you along with the instrument, or do you tend to find the musical idea once at the instrument?It really depends, but when speaking about producing the score for , I naturally came to the idea of using synthesizers for most of the score, and the piano should stay as occasional use, after watching the film. Because I think this film has a lot of ambiguity showing different kinds of emotions and you can’t really define who is good or bad actually. And I think that electronic sounds are well suited to expressing subtle aspects of human psychology, while an acoustic instrument like the piano, the nature of the instrument can be quite strong, so I feel it can sometimes limit the kind of impression or feeling it creates. So I kept the use of the piano to a minimum, using it instead at key points in the story, and I think it worked quite well.What was your studio setup for ? What instruments/gear/software did you use to make the album?Since the music was specifically composed to be performed live as a solo piece, the setup was quite minimal as listed below:- Small modular setup - Mutable Instruments’ oscillator Plaits, Doepfer’s LFO A-145 and Morphagene by Make Noise- Strymon Bigsky reverb pedalAround 60% of the album was made using only with MiniFreak, with 9-10 different presets. I altered their sound characteristics using the filters. For track 8 “Take Me With You,“ I used only Plaits as the sound source. I connected a sine-wave LFO to Plaits’ Level input and used the LFO’s dynamics and intervals to slowly evolve the timbre.And at the beginning of the track 9 “Mother’s Path,“ I kept a piano phrase recorded with Morphagene looping, while using its granular capabilities to significantly transform the sound. All sounds from both modules were routed through the Bigsky.To produce the album, I recorded everything in Abelton Live and made some subtle EQ adjustments there, while also adding a minimum amount of reverb using Valhalla plugins. As I was already happy with my initial compositions I’ve made for the premiere concert, I tried not to change them too much and instead focused more on mixing, especially with the last track “Forever In The Sky“ where I used Plugin Boutique’s Stereo Savage to expand and deepen the stereo panning.What's it like composing for a film, versus creating your own original music?When composing for a film, you usually have a director who often has certain musical ideas that you need to realize. But when creating your own music, you can do whatever you want, so this is obviously the main difference. But for me, sometimes having musical limitations or being asked to work within someone else’s ideas can actually help me find a new way of approaching things, both technically and creatively.But the situation with was a little different from a usual scoring project, as the music was composed genuinely for live performance. I had complete creative freedom, while the music of course still needed to work well with the story. That was actually the only real limitation I had, and it gave me a lot of inspiration. I’m very thankful to VIERNULVIER for giving me this special opportunity.How do you discover new music these days? Any recent notable finds?I often discover new music while exploring Bandcamp or some random websites, or otherwise at concerts or record stores. The record I recently stumbled upon and bought is Helen Money’s . This album is already a couple of years old, but I’m happy I found it now, thanks to the shop Bis Aufs Messer in Berlin. I really enjoyed the beautiful, massive sound of her cello.Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.I think everyone has a different idea of what makes someone underrated, but if I had to name one, I’d say Natalie Beridze. There’s always a real strength at the core of her sound, and at times, it also has a sense of spaciousness and warmth. I enjoy almost everything she makes.What are you working on next?Since I’m releasing two albums this year, and I’ve released quite a few albums and worked on several scoring projects over the past few years as well, I feel like I’d like to focus more on playing live as much as possible for a while, rather than making new music.

item.title: Song Battle: Judas Priest – “Breaking the Law” vs. Iron Maiden – “Run to the Hills”
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: Two songs. Two bands. Two completely different approaches to heavy metal.Judas Priest’s “Breaking the Law” and Iron Maiden’s “Run to the Hills” are among the most recognizable songs in the history of British heavy metal, but they get there in very different ways.“Breaking the Law” is short, blunt and almost ridiculously simple. It takes one of the greatest metal guitar riffs ever recorded, adds Rob Halford’s unmistakable voice and gets out of the way before it has a chance to overstay its welcome.“Run to the Hills” is bigger, faster and considerably more ambitious. Bruce Dickinson’s vocals soar over Steve Harris’s galloping bass lines while Dave Murray and Adrian Smith provide the guitars that helped define Iron Maiden’s sound.One is a compact metal sledgehammer.The other is a full-speed metal charge.Both became defining songs for their respective bands. Both helped establish the sound of British heavy metal in the early 1980s.Song Profile: “Breaking the Law”Released in 1980 on Judas Priest’s , “Breaking the Law” is one of those songs where the simplicity is the entire point.The opening guitar riff is immediately recognizable. K.K. Downing and Glenn Tipton don’t need a complicated arrangement to make an impact. The riff is repetitive, muscular and incredibly effective.Rob Halford’s vocal performance is equally direct. Instead of relying on the high-pitched screams that would become one of his trademarks, Halford delivers the song with a controlled, almost conversational menace.“Breaking the law” repeated over and over shouldn’t work as well as it does.The song is barely three minutes long, and there isn’t a second of wasted space. The guitars establish the hook, Halford delivers the attitude, the rhythm section keeps everything moving and the song disappears almost as quickly as it arrived.That economy is a huge part of its appeal.Judas Priest didn’t need to demonstrate everything they could do.They just needed one riff.Song Profile: “Run to the Hills”Iron Maiden’s “Run to the Hills” arrived in 1982 on , and it immediately demonstrated how much bigger and more elaborate Maiden’s approach to heavy metal had become.Steve Harris’s galloping bass line is the engine driving the entire song. The guitars add melodic harmonies and rapid-fire riffs while Clive Burr’s drumming gives the track its relentless momentum.And then there is Bruce Dickinson.His vocal performance is one of the song’s defining features. He moves from aggressive verses into soaring, high-energy passages that make the song feel enormous.“Run to the Hills” also has more structural movement than “Breaking the Law.” It builds, shifts gears and creates the sensation of constantly moving forward.Where Judas Priest went for maximum impact with minimum ingredients, Iron Maiden packed considerably more musical information into the song.It is heavier, faster and more technically demanding.“Breaking the Law” is a masterclass in economy.The riff is immediately memorable, the structure is easy to follow and the chorus is impossible to forget.But “Run to the Hills” is considerably more ambitious. The arrangement moves between contrasting sections while maintaining a strong central hook. Harris builds the song around that galloping rhythm and gives the guitars plenty of room to add melodic detail.“Breaking the Law” is incredibly efficient.“Run to the Hills” is more developed.Priest gets maximum results from minimal ingredients, but Maiden’s songwriting is more sophisticated.This is a battle between two of heavy metal’s greatest singers.Rob Halford’s performance on “Breaking the Law” is remarkably restrained. He doesn’t need to scream his way through the song. His delivery gives the track an attitude that makes the lyrics feel almost casually rebellious.Bruce Dickinson takes the opposite approach.His performance on “Run to the Hills” is explosive. The high notes, aggression and sheer range make the vocal one of the song’s most memorable elements.Dickinson is spectacular.Dickinson’s performance gives Maiden the edge.This may be the closest round of the entire battle.“Breaking the Law” has one of the most recognizable guitar riffs in metal history. You don’t need the drums, bass or vocals. Give someone the riff and they immediately know the song.“Run to the Hills” has several excellent guitar parts, including its famous galloping passages and harmonized sections.But this isn’t really close.The Priest riff is one of those riffs that has escaped the boundaries of heavy metal and become part of popular culture.Judas Priest takes this round easily.Round 4: Bass & Rhythm Section“Breaking the Law” has a tight, straightforward rhythm section that serves the guitar riff perfectly.But Iron Maiden has Steve Harris.Harris’s bass isn’t simply sitting underneath the guitars. It drives “Run to the Hills.” That galloping bass style became one of the defining characteristics of Iron Maiden’s sound.Clive Burr matches him with rapid, energetic drumming that keeps the entire track moving at a furious pace.Maiden’s rhythm section is doing considerably more work.“Breaking the Law” is energetic, but its power comes from its stomp.It feels like a fist coming straight at you.“Run to the Hills” feels like being chased by that fist.The galloping rhythm creates constant forward momentum, and the drums and guitars make the song feel like it is accelerating even when the tempo itself remains controlled.The Maiden track simply has more velocity.For sheer adrenaline, Iron Maiden takes it.This is another round where simplicity wins.“Breaking the law” is one of those choruses that requires absolutely no explanation. Even someone who has never heard the entire song probably knows what comes next once the riff starts.“Run to the Hills” has a fantastic chorus, but it is more dependent on Dickinson’s vocal performance and the surrounding arrangement.The Priest chorus is practically a chant.And it sticks in your head immediately.Judas Priest wins on pure memorability.“British Steel” has a relatively stripped-down production compared with the increasingly elaborate metal records that followed it.That works perfectly for “Breaking the Law.” Everything is clear, punchy and focused around the riff. gives “Run to the Hills” a much bigger sound. The guitars have more dimension, the drums hit harder and Dickinson’s vocals dominate the track.The Maiden production makes the song feel enormous.The larger production suits Maiden’s bigger musical approach.Both songs helped define their bands.“Breaking the Law” took heavy metal’s basic ingredients and stripped them down to an almost punk-like simplicity. It proved that metal didn’t always need lengthy guitar solos or complicated arrangements to be effective.“Run to the Hills” helped establish another side of the genre: melodic, ambitious and technically demanding heavy metal.Iron Maiden’s approach was more distinctive.The galloping bass, harmonized guitars and Dickinson’s vocals created a sound that was unmistakably Maiden.Maiden gets the edge for creating a more distinctive musical identity within the song.“Breaking the Law” is one of the songs that immediately comes to mind when people think of classic heavy metal.The music video became famous for its ridiculous bank robbery storyline, while the song itself became a permanent part of Judas Priest’s live repertoire.But “Run to the Hills” had an enormous impact too.It became one of Iron Maiden’s signature songs and helped make one of the landmark albums of the New Wave of British Heavy Metal.Both songs became gateways into metal for generations of listeners.But Priest’s song has one advantage.You don’t even have to be a metal fan to recognize it.The riff and chorus have become almost universally recognizable.Round 10: Overall Metal FactorThis is where the battle gets interesting.“Breaking the Law” represents one of metal’s greatest strengths: simplicity.It’s loud, aggressive, memorable and impossible to mistake for anything else.“Run to the Hills” represents another side of metal: speed, musicianship, melodic guitar work, powerful vocals and a sense of scale.If “Breaking the Law” is the guy standing in the parking lot with a leather jacket and a guitar riff, “Run to the Hills” is the guy charging over the hill on horseback with an entire army behind him.But if we’re judging which song packs more of the genre’s defining characteristics into one track, Maiden has the advantage.Iron Maiden takes the final round.Breaking the Law — 4 roundsRun to the Hills — 6 roundsThe Winner: “Run to the Hills”Iron Maiden takes the battle, but Judas Priest absolutely makes them work for it.“Breaking the Law” might actually be the more instantly recognizable song. Its guitar riff is legendary, its chorus is ridiculously catchy and its short running time makes it almost impossible to get tired of.But “Run to the Hills” does more.The songwriting is more ambitious. The rhythm section is more dynamic. The vocals are more demanding. The guitars are more elaborate. And the entire performance feels like it is operating at maximum speed.Judas Priest perfected the metal .Iron Maiden perfected the metal .“Breaking the Law” is the song you hear once and immediately remember.“Run to the Hills” is the song that makes you want to turn the volume up.And when these two giants go head-to-head, that extra musical firepower gives Iron Maiden the victory.Winner: Iron Maiden — “Run to the Hills”

item.title: The Tree
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Simon's cat climbed too high in a tree and it turns out the way you would expect. I had a problem with Sundae doing this when she was a half-grown kitten. Three times that year she got stuck high in a tree and sat there for a day or two waiting for someone to rescue her. Three different guys went up three different extension ladders. They were all more afraid of being injured by Sundae than they were afraid of heights. They just removed her from the tree and dropped her. The third time was the charm, when Sundae learned once and for all that she can fall from that height and land safely.

item.title: Qwen3.8 27B addition in words
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded:
Colin Frasier posted on Bluesky about an experiment he ran over two years ago using GPT-4o to see how well it could "compute the sum but return the answer in words" across increasingly large numbers. Here's the chart he shared of those results:I'm confident GPT-4o didn't cheat and use a calculator, especially since it got so many of the calculations wrong, but I was inspired to run the experiment again on local hardware (a DGX Spark) to explore the effect in a fully controlled environment.I pasted his image into a Codex Remote session (GPT-6 Astra) and had it run the same experiment using . Here's the result for a run of 30 attempts per combination with reasoning disabled:Then I ran it again with reasoning enabled. This took a per pair, so instead of running 30 samples per square I ran just one - which results in a much less visually appealing heatmap since each square is either 100% or 0%:It got the right answer in 167 out of 169 attempts, and since these were one-shot I'm confident a second run would produce different results here.Here's a version of the report that includes the reasoning traces from some of those larger calculations, which include text like this:Wait, let me redo this more carefully.
4,299,366,105,622 6,088,794,067,970
Let me align them: 4 2 9 9 3 6 6 1 0 5 6 2 2 6 0 8 8 7 9 4 0 6 7 9 7 0
Adding from right to left: Position 1 (units): 2 + 0 = 2 Position 2 (tens): 2 + 7 = 9 Position 3 (hundreds): 6 + 9 = 15, write 5, carry 1

item.title: Herbie
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Herbie is a triangular cat. He came from an animal shelter with a rare condition that makes his ears stick out to the sides instead of standing up on his head, leaving him looking somewhat like Dobby the house elf. He can't move his ears. But even more concerning is that Herbie is unable to close his eyes! He doesn't blink, and he sleeps with his eyes open, although his third eyelid does give him some protection. Herbie was diagnosed with bilateral facial nerve paralysis. He also has mild cerebellar hypoplasia, so he needs a special human to look after him. His foster mother became an expert at caring for him and now he's a permanent member of the family. You can see more of Herbie at Instagram.

item.title: They Packed The Trop And Were Treated To A Gem
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: Bryan Baker, closer for the Tampa Bay Rays, encountered a new problem on the mound Saturday night. He'd been summoned to record the final three outs of Game 1 of the ALDS and to preserve and finish a franchise all-timer of a gem from teammate Drew Rasmussen, who'd pitched eight shutout innings of miraculous one-hit baseball against the New York Yankees' depleted but still fearsome lineup.Baker, working out pitch-sequencing with catcher Liam Hicks, found that he was having trouble making out the sounds coming from the little PitchCom speaker buzzing right next to his ear. After a 1–1 fastball nicked the outside of the zone against pinch hitter Giancarlo Stanton, Baker had to cup his glove over his ear to hear the call."That was probably the most electric crowd I've ever played in front of," Baker said after the game, a 1–0 Rays victory. "Still kind of digesting it."

item.title: Ty France And The Padres Thwarted By Good Old Reality
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: Ty France talks like a guy who is pretty sure he'd socked a game-winning dinger. "I stood there and watched it, and it was going," France said Saturday, of his ninth-inning moonshot. "It was staying fair." The ball did, in fact, stay fair: Soaring down the left field line, France's fly bonked off a roof cable and dropped, well inside fair territory and directly into the glove of Milwaukee's Jackson Chourio, for San Diego's second out of the ninth inning. France stood in disbelief, peering and pointing at the approximate spot where his heroic moment was thwarted by an impermeable ceiling. The umpires got together, discussed the stadium's ground rules, and came to a pretty quick conclusion: The ball was fair when it bonked, and thus in play when it fell, and Chourio caught it, and France was out. The Padres went on to lose, 3–2. Sorry. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T6a-SnWptd0

item.title: Preznit Fuckwit: still a moron, still insane, still a loser. Let us count the ways.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Film legend Barbara Stanwyck once famously quipped that her only professional challenge was “finding a way to play my fortieth fallen female in a different way from my thirty-ninth.”Those of us who spend our lives reporting on the infantile antics of the pants-shittingest piss-baby ever to crap himself raw in the Oval Bordello have a similar issue. With Dear Leader’s firehose of malignant fuckery spraying directly into our faces, twenty-four-seven, how do we keep that shit fresh? How do we find some new angle on the madness, and not repeat ourselves?“We’re gonna win big, and we’re gonna shove it up their ass.”Oh, how charming. That was Donny, at a campaign rally last night in Vandalia, Ohio — and he’s closing the deal by promising that will get . How nice! Donny’s rancid anus-mouth has always been a ticking time bomb — but at least he kind of used to keep it barely civil, . Not any more. His rapidly-advancing dementia has collapsed his cortex to the point where all the filters have gone . Now, you never know how low Donny might go. So we’ve got that going for us.“And we will pass— the DEATH penalty for large scale drug dealers, human traffickers, and anyone— who EVER KILLS a police officer, or law enforcement official.”Again, that was Donny, last night in Ohio — but it could have been any one of his campaign rallies, at any time during the last decade. Donny’s been making the same worn-out promises, over and over — and has followed though on none of them, despite holding majorities in the House and the Senate. How many times has this fucker promised that his glorious health care plan will be ready in two weeks? Same with infrastructure. How many times? I have no idea, because I can’t count that high.But look at all the cultists standing behind Dear Leader, jumping for joy and pumping their fists as he makes the exact same promise to KILL EVERYONE that he made in 2016. Does MAGA even remember that they’ve been cheering for the same empty words, over and over? I’m guessing — because massive head trauma doesn’t magically cure itself overnight.So how do you find some new angle to report on that shit? Unfortunately, until someone comes out with a movie about some homie who can no longer form lasting memories, it’s going to be the dude from Memento, .Oh, and before any of you smart-asses pipes up with, ‘but Uncle Jeff, what about Fifty First Dates,’ let me just point out that no one remembers that flick even exists.Don’t you love how Donny makes every campaign appearance about himself? Last night’s speech was ostensibly in support of Vivek Ramaswamy — but if you blinked at the wrong time, you missed the nanosecond where Dear Leader mentioned Vivek, before launching back into some incomprehensible Shakespearean soliloquy about “and just yesterday, Bayer— I love their aspirin, I take an aspirin a day. I don’t know if it works but psychologically I need it. It thins the hell out of your blood, I guess. I don’t know if it works or not but I’ve been doing it for a long time. And here I am making speeches. Bayer— and I LIKE BAYER aspirin. Little, yellow— and I take the big one. You know they want me to go down to the eighty. I take the three-hundred and— eighty six, I don’t know what the hell it is. It's a monster. They said, ‘SIR YOU DON’T NEED THAT!’ I said, do me a favor, I’ve been doing okay for 35 years. Leave me alone.”But tell me, after sitting through that meandering dollop of dumbfuckery, do you think MAGA even remembers who they’re supposed to be voting for?Well, just to be a dick about it, I’m going to drop in a meme from Fifty First Dates, and you’re all going to go,Yeah, I have no fucking clue what that’s about, either. Like you, I’ve never seen Fifty First Dates. That why we keep falling back on Memento.I’m sorry, what we were even talking about? Oh yeah, right — Dear Leader’s batshit campaign speech. Sorry, I keep drifting off.“We will pass the No Invasion of Our Country ACT— prohibiting any future president from ever opening our borders to illegal immigrants again. What? We will pass a truly great healthcare plan.”Yeah, None of that shit is going to happen. Donny’s nonsensical promise to magically pass legislation he hasn’t been competent enough to have already passed is no different from Donny sitting down with bankers and investors back in 1984 and promising that his planned Atlantic City casinos were going to make everyone rich.Tell me, how did that work out for everyone who fell for the slick patter of Donny the flim-flam man?Donny’s just chock-full of bullshit. Always has been, always will be.The bottom line is that who gives a shit what memes I use to mock the fuckery. All that matters is that Donny is super toxic right now. He’s massively unpopular — even among the GOP — and every time he shows up at one of these shittacular rallies, he just digs himself and his party deeper. Shoot that shit straight into my veins.Get out and vote on November 3rd. It’ll ruin Donny’s day. I promise.After all that, I think we’ve earned ourselves some Daily Claudia. Wouldn’t you agree?Here’s a trio of Ms Spouse, enjoying a boating excursion on the Hudson River near Rhinebeck, on July 15, 2017.Have a great Sunday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: My brain on a Sunday morning
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: I was on my Mac this morning, just minding my own business, when suddenly I found myself using the Linux laptop, and I liked it.On Sunday mornings, I do system maintenance. This means running updates on all my computers. Right now, that's five machines: one Linux desktop, two Linux laptops, one Mac desktop, and one Mac laptop. Yes, that's too many, but it is what it is.Both Linux laptops run CachyOS, which is Arch-based, so there are updates.I started with the Framework. Once it was updated and rebooted, I pulled the latest tweaks to my Emacs config, to make sure it worked on Linux. I've been leaning toward using macOS exclusively, so I haven't been testing things on Linux as much. Everything worked, though.While typing on the Framework, the first thing I thought about was how much I prefer typing on it to typing on the MacBook Air. Then I remembered how much I like the of Linux. Then I noticed that Emacs starts up more than twice as fast on the Framework for some reason. Then I remembered that the best (and only) way to have consistent Emacs key bindings on Linux is to, well, use Emacs.All this to say that the conflict between running macOS, Linux, or both is still a thing. As troublesome and complex as it can be, I think the answer will always be "both". Surely I can manage it, right? Maybe if I only use the laptops for simple things like blogging, browsing, or journaling, things will be easy enough. I'll never be able to settle on one or the other. Just admit it.I'm on the couch typing this in Emacs using the Framework, both things I told myself a week ago that I'd stop doing. My stupid brain is always mucking things up.

item.title: You've stood with me. Here's what's next.
item.author: 1axbkddtc87p0ndwzoslnw6i979x1i1ymvs1ib@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Election Day is 30 days away, and the fight for free and fair elections is here. In some states, early voting has already begun, and nearly every state has sent out mail-in ballots.I have been on the road the last week traveling. I apologize that some of my essays have been shorter and videos less well-produced.For months, we have been building toward this moment. Campaigns are communicating with voters and executing get-out-the-vote plans. Nonprofit groups are registering voters and recruiting poll workers.Then there are the lawyers. My law firm is currently litigating nearly 90 voting and election cases in more than 40 states. We have beaten the Department of Justice more than 20 times, defended voting by mail against Trump's executive orders, and won three times at the Supreme Court to keep Missouri from using an illegally gerrymandered map.But that is only part of the fight.Democracy Docket is tracking almost 200 cases in nearly all 50 states and D.C. Keeping a spotlight on what is happening to democracy in the courts is a critical part of the effort to protect our elections.Since Trump returned to office, Democracy Docket has closely tracked his authoritarian schemes. While other media outlets have bent the knee, Democracy Docket has remained unbowed.I created Democracy Docket for moments like this. And you, our readers, have been with me the entire time.When I'm tired, your words energize me. Your support helps me fight another day. I will never forget that.No matter what happens on Election Day, and no matter what Trump does or threatens, I promise you this: Democracy Docket will keep fighting.As a subscriber, you know that everything on the Democracy Docket website and in its flagship newsletters is available to everyone. All its reporting and video content is free.What you may not know is that Democracy Docket also offers a premium membership for people who want deeper analysis. Premium members receive my exclusive analysis and are invited to member-only briefings and events.Most importantly, premium members sustain Democracy Docket's independent, pro-democracy mission. It has no corporate parent or investors. There are no venture capitalists or private equity backers. It does not rely on ActBlue or Substack.To put it simply, it relies on you.With Election Day right around the corner, we will have to work harder than ever. If you haven't upgraded to a premium membership, please consider doing so today. Become part of the community that powers Democracy Docket's work and protects our democracy.If now isn't the right moment for you, I understand, and I thank you for being a loyal reader. Every one of you is an important part of our team and of this mission.We are all in this fight together, and I couldn't do it without you. We have an important fight ahead in just 30 days, but I know we will win — together.

item.title: Steven Spielberg's new film is his best in decades
item.content:encoded: I put a question to my SFGATE colleagues just the other day that had them mulling for a bit: What’s the last great movie that Steven Spielberg directed? I’m not talking about a merely film. The old man can put together a competent picture anytime he likes. I’m talking about an all-timer of a Spielberg movie, something that belongs up there with his best work, which includes “Jaws,” “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” “E.T.,” “Schindler’s List” and … you get the idea. When you’re a director who’s made not just one of the greatest movies of all time but of them, audience members like me hope for (and oftentimes ) greatness from you with every subsequent project. Such is the standard that Spielberg, father of the modern blockbuster, set for himself. It’s also a standard that, in my opinion, he has not reached since the release of “Catch Me If You Can,” his note-perfect caper film, back in 2002. The bulk of my colleagues agreed, which led to a much more pointed question: Is Steven Spielberg washed?With the release this week of his latest movie, “Disclosure Day,” I can now tell you, the reader, that the answer is no. Steven Spielberg, much to my relief, is still very much Steven Spielberg. This is the best film he’s made in nearly a quarter century. I have no idea if it’ll ascend to the status of an enduring classic — only time gets to decide that—but goddamn, what a movie.If you’re unfamiliar with the premise of “Disclosure Day,” perhaps because it has a clunky title that reminds viewers like me of that one time Demi Moore sexually harassed Michael Douglas, I can get you situated real quick (and relatively spoiler-free). Steven Spielberg has made another movie about extraterrestrials. That’s really all you need to know, isn’t it? You know that Spielberg is in his element when he’s spinning a yarn about little green men from outer space. It’s a subject that aligns perfectly with his directorial sensibilities: the wonder of the unknown, the idea that we are not alone, kids who have serious daddy issues, things of that nature. So long as you’re not watching “Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull,” you know that your alien story is in good hands with this man.Article continues below this adThis time around, our story is about Daniel Kellner (rising star Josh O’Connor), a pencil-pusher at a shadowy defense corporation who opens the film having stolen a precious MacGuffin, among other things, from his boss Noah Scanlon (Colin Firth). You know what big meanies the men in suits are in a Spielberg flick. Firth, operating at peak Colin Firth, plays his character no different. Scanlon wants his MacGuffin back and sends out a legion of underlings in black cars to capture Kellner and blow stuff up real good.Meanwhile, a flighty weatherlady in Kansas City named Margaret Fairchild (Emily Blunt, flawless) sees a red cardinal fly into her apartment one day, and suddenly, she can read minds, speak fluent Korean and involuntarily break out into alien clucks in the middle of a live broadcast. Blunt’s weatherlady gets visions of O’Connor’s Kellner in her head and feels the urgent need to go to him despite having no idea where he is. At the same time, Kellner has to get the extraterrestrial artifact he stole from the bad men in suits to the only good one he knows (Oscar nominee Colman Domingo), who appears to be hiding out inside a studio soundstage somewhere in the Midwest. There’s also a lapsed nun played by Bono’s daughter.Article continues below this adBy now, you’re already asking me, “Hey man, where are the goddamn aliens in all this?” Well, turns out that Firth’s bad guy has been overseeing a government plot to not only suppress evidence of close encounters of the third kind here on Earth but also video footage of the U.S. government doing unspeakable things to those aliens and exploiting their extraterrestrial resources for questionable purposes. Pick the allegory of your choice from that morsel. O’Connor not only wants the government to pay for his atrocities but also wants to “disclose,” on a single “day,” all of these secrets to the world at large.This is where the Spielberg difference is most prevalent. Any movie can stage a 2.5-hour chase for some ET microfiche, but Spielberg (credited here with the screen story) uses the concept of a disclosure day to ask deeper questions. Can humankind handle this knowledge? Will people accept the existence of aliens, especially in a time of deepfakes? they accept it, especially if the aliens in question are a superior life-form? Could humans adopt this life-form as their new god and throw out all of the old religions? Spielberg makes time, all throughout “Disclosure Day,” to hammer away at these unanswerable questions. He also makes sure to throw in a brilliant comic sequence about how hard it is to run over your own cellphone with a sedan. All of that detail gives the action sequences much higher stakes than a cookie-cutter tentpole movie would. Article continues below this adAnd those action sequences kick ass, especially a brilliant train crash sequence that perfectly echoes a toy train crash sequence from his movie, the autobiographical “The Fabelmans.” I didn’t pee once during “Disclosure Day.” Didn’t even think about doing it. I was way too invested in what was going to happen to all of the characters in it, and to humanity as a result. A lot of summer blockbusters tell you that the fate of humankind hangs in the balance. Here’s a movie that actually shows you that view from the precipice. So when we finally reach the movie’s climax, you, the viewer, are just as riveted by what’s unfolding as the characters are.This isn’t a perfect movie. Spielberg holds off on his cornier instincts for the bulk of “Disclosure Day” but eventually dips into the simple syrup. Firth misses his dead wife. O’Connor and Blunt miss their respective lost childhoods. A kiddie actor encounters a bunch of friendly CGI animals (my daughter said they looked like AI) and then walks into a super bright light. That, too, you expect from a Spielberg picture. After all, “Jaws” was the last utterly unsentimental movie he made, and that was half a century ago. But for “Disclosure Day,” Spielberg reins in those impulses as best he can and delivers not only one of the best movies of the summer but the best film that he himself has made in decades. The old man’s still got it, and we’re lucky to have him.Article continues below this ad

item.title: Congratulations, the Reflecting Pool is now a swamp
item.content:encoded: The one thing that Washington, D.C., has always had going for it is its beauty. The people who run America from this town have always been an unsightly bunch, but they’ve done their nasty work in a city that has acquired, over the course of this country’s lifespan, an aesthetic like no other. No other major American city looks as regally beautiful as D.C. You and I have a long-standing federal law to thank for this, but we also have a collection of national landmarks clustered in the center of the district that the aforementioned law was written to both protect and to showcase. The Capitol. The Lincoln Memorial. The Washington Monument. These are gorgeous edifices, ones designed to outlast old generations and to inspire newer ones. They are the best of D.C., and therefore the best of America.Not content to let an army of UFC slobs desecrate the capital this past weekend, nor to personally oversee the physical ruination of the White House earlier this year, Trump has now decided to destroy the humble Reflecting Pool along the National Mall. You’ve probably heard about the Reflecting Pool situation: how President Cronyism dished out a no-bid contract to renovate the pool earlier this spring to a company that had done work at his Virginia golf club, how the project came in over budget (big surprise), and how the results have turned out disastrously, with algae blooms overtaking the pool within moments of its unveiling. Article continues below this adBecause I’m a rubbernecker by nature, on Tuesday I decided to head down to the National Mall to see the damage myself. Come with me now on a quick trip to a national treasure that has now become the world’s dullest aquarium.Article continues below this adIt’s a gorgeous day to visit the mall. The weather outside is flawless and, because it’s a Tuesday, tourist traffic is at a relative minimum. Normally, this would be an ideal day to sit by the Reflecting Pool and meditate on freedom, democracy and other quaint notions. But the second I make my way into the heart of the mall, between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II Memorial, I see an expanse of wet, sickly green. Like the ocean on a bad day. I have never seen the Reflecting Pool look this ugly. Trump’s goal with this renovation was to paint the bottom of the pool “American flag blue,” an idiotic idea because this pool is specifically not supposed to be ANY color. Previous administrations have kept the water here clean and clear so that it can, you know, reflect, so that visitors could look into the pool’s waters and see in it the royal blue sky, the wedding cake white clouds, the stately gray monument on the hill next door. You’re not supposed to look into this pool and see anything but the surrounding splendor, your pretty little face included.When I look into the pool now, I see nothing but green murk. The algae is still here, and it’s still defeating Trump’s cleanup crews handily. One of those crews is working a corner of the pool near the Lincoln Memorial. They’re all National Park Service staffers, overseen by Trump’s metaphorical pool boy Doug Burgum. One of them orders the others, “Let’s get this hose in the water and be sure not to twist it.” The hose is attached to a small, roving pool vacuum. It’s not a fair fight, unkinked hose or no. Just a few weeks ago, Trump was bragging that this pool was “bigger than skyscrapers.” He even made a definitely scientifically accurate chart to prove the point. Turns out that hugeness can really bite you in the ass when your very large and strong pool has an infestation problem.Article continues below this adI walk along the esplanade, and more Park Service crews mar the view. I see a couple more vacuums. Even uglier, I see a number of hoses languishing in the pool, looking like the tentacles of some evil monster and spewing a white foam into the depths. These machines are presumably the “nanobubblers” that the Park Service, perhaps now helmed by Russell Wilson, claims have “successfully destroyed the algae bloom.” They have not. All they appear to be doing is troubling the water enough so that it has an even less reflective quality. I’d have better odds seeing my reflection in a cinder block.I kneel by the pool and dip my hand into the water. Thankfully, my flesh doesn’t instantly dissolve upon contact with it. I feel along the inside of the pool, and it’s slimy to the touch. Six years ago, I bought our family an inflatable hot tub to stave off boredom during the COVID-19 pandemic, another Trump production. I didn’t know anything about pool maintenance, so the water in that hot tub also turned green, and the insides of it were slimy in the exact same way the pool’s insides are right now. I can be forgiven for my negligence back then, because I was a bored rookie. When you’re the richest nation in world history, you don’t deserve quite as much slack.Article continues below this adI take my hand out of the water and lick my fingers. The water tastes fine. If I end up hospitalized with diphtheria later tonight, my editors will update this post accordingly.I continue walking the esplanade, and the water only gets dirtier. In one corner, the pool looks like it’s been the victim of a gasoline spill. There’s a lone duckling swimming around in this failed Jackson Pollock work, and I desperately want to fish it out with a net and help it find its mommy.Then I look over to the nearby World War II Memorial. Opened in 2004, this memorial features a fountain pool at its center, flanked by 50 pillars representing fallen combat veterans from every state. And wouldn’t you know it, the fountain pool is pristine. We’re literally feet away from the befouled Reflecting Pool, and the difference is staggering. I can see reflections in this other pool! Some of them blue! I see tourists happily dipping their bare feet into its waters! I see an American landmark that looks the way it’s supposed to look, the way these landmarks always looked until Trump and his power frown came along to destroy it all.Article continues below this adI walk back to my car. Along the way I cross through the Constitution Gardens, which boasts its own serene pond. The water in this pond is dirtier than the WWII monument’s water, but it’s still unscathed by the algae blooms. I edge closer to the pond and see a family of ducks, little baby ducklings included, frolicking happily in the water. These ducks are smart. They know the good stuff when they see it. Maybe we should let them run this city.

item.title: Brandon Aiyuk's NFL career is already over
item.content:encoded: The NFL has had itself one miserable offseason. You may have been too busy watching America self-immolating to notice, but the football men have been behaving incredibly badly of late. Falcons edge rusher James Pearce got arrested for allegedly being a psycho boyfriend to Chicago Sky forward Rickea Jackson. The Denver Broncos have a sudden, and grotesque, DV problem on their hands. Terrion Arnold just got dropped by the Lions after being arrested on suspicion of kidnapping. And New England coach Mike Vrabel can’t seem to keep his little Pat Patriot in his trousers. All of it either has been ugly or has served as a portent of more ugliness to come. Which brings us to the curious story of 49ers wideout Brandon Aiyuk, whose recent behavior has gone from maddening to outright frightening. Just two years ago, Aiyuk re-upped with the team after posting a career-high 1,342 receiving yards, making All-Pro and helping the Niners reach the Super Bowl the season prior. Wideouts tend to be mercurial in nature, but they also represent one of the highest-value non-QB positions in the NFL, right up there alongside left tackles and edge rushers. So when the Niners braintrust gave Aiyuk his money after the usual contentious negotiation phase, no one could really blame it. Paying Aiyuk ensured that he, alongside QB Brock Purdy, would keep the team in contention through the rest of the decade. Two years later … The above video represents perhaps the world’s saddest attempt at making it rain. It’s also just one in a series of Insta posts from Aiyuk that, taken in aggregate, are more distressing than they are laughable. Aiyuk played only half a season after his contract extension, tearing his knee up midway through the 2024 campaign and then ghosting on the team entirely in 2025. Throughout all of this, Aiyuk has been posting videos of himself driving at Jose Canseco speeds, calling the Niners stupid, demanding the team cut him so that he can sign with the Washington Commanders (no word on if the Commanders are actually open to the prospect, and signs are pointing to the contrary), and finally threatening to whip the entire organization with a belt: Article continues below this ad“They running from that belt that’s on the way. It’s inevitable. It’s coming. Stop running.” Normally I’d consider the “belt” in a quote like this to be metaphorical. But in this case, I cannot discount the possibility that yes, Brandon Aiyuk would like to physically remove his belt and assault Niners personnel with it. Because his behavior over the past two years has gone well beyond the usual “the enemy speaks kindly & holds a knife” genre of posting that you and I usually get from our nation’s disgruntled wideout population. Aiyuk has openly taunted Bay Area law enforcement to come arrest him, fired his agent for being too cozy with Niners GM John Lynch, posted cryptic pleas to the NFLPA for being too cozy with that agent, and accused Lynch of showing up at his house unannounced, stalker-style. I am not a doctor, but I’ve been around long enough to recognize when someone is behaving in a deeply unwell manner online. Donald Trump is unwell online. These AI evangelists are unwell online. And Brandon Aiyuk is unwell online. In most circumstances, NFL teams have been willing to overlook this kind of s—t. Hell, your own Niners gainfully employed Terrell Owens for many years, despite the fact that TO was a galactic asswipe (who made homophobic comments to boot). In fact, the NFL serves as perhaps our most visible example of what Americans say they won’t tolerate versus what they won’t tolerate. There isn’t a set of hard criteria for this, of course. If there were, our Supreme Court would already be a pile of ashes by now. Oh, to dream. Article continues below this adBut it’s telling that Aiyuk’s behavior has rendered him radioactive across the league at the same time that Terrion Arnold’s legal trouble proved too much for the Lions to withstand, and that erstwhile Texas Tech QB Brendan Sorsby was denied entry in the NFL’s supplemental draft after he was outed as a severe gambling addict. The league will only let you hang around if you’re either too expensive to get rid of (Deshaun Watson) or not worth the trouble at any price. Given that San Francisco has already partially voided Aiyuk’s deal, and given that no other franchise has expressed any interest in taking him on, the wideout has clearly fallen into the latter category. If there were any sign that his mental state was improving, he’d be on another team’s roster right now. He’s not, and it’s fair to speculate that his behavior — what’s been made public about it and what’s probably been going around the league’s sprawling gossip network about it — has been so alarming that no one in the NFL dare preside over his further descent into madness. And I mean ever. Not this coming season, and not in any season to come. The man’s career is over. This is tragic from a mercenary perspective; the guy could ball when he was inclined to. But it now feels tragic in a much more general sense. I can’t tell you what exactly is wrong with Brandon Aiyuk. But I can tell you that if the NFL wants nothing to do with him, it’s worse than any of us can probably imagine.Article continues below this ad

item.title: It's easy to blame the USMNT's World Cup crashout on one man. So I will.
item.content:encoded: Much like our nation itself, the World Cup run for the U.S. men’s national soccer team started off promisingly, only to become a sick joke. The USMNT got eliminated from the 2026 Cup on Monday night after Belgium crushed it 4-1, in a game where the home team was thoroughly outplayed, outclassed and outcoached. But if the loss itself stung, the context in which it was played only made it feel that much worse. Yes, that backstory includes Donald Trump, but to a small degree, it also involves USMNT poster child and possible Trump fanboy Christian Pulisic. The first man disgraced the team off the field. The second man disgraced the team on it. How did all of this come to pass? Well, I suppose it’s my job to explain it, although the prospect of doing so excites about as much as having my legs ripped clean off my body. This year’s USMNT was, by a few tangible measures, better than any other in recent memory. The U.S. won its group for only the third time in team history. It won two games in group play, which the USMNT had never done before, and by an aggregate score of 6-1. In fact, only three teams scored more goals than the USMNT in group play this tournament. Most important, the Americans LOOKED like they belonged. I’ve usually had to cheer for U.S. men’s teams that only had a spare handful of players who could cut it as pros abroad. Those teams would inevitably get bounced out of the elimination stages, if not much earlier, by one of the real soccer countries. Article continues below this adBut in group play, this USMNT featured players who had international pro cred, including Pulisic (currently with AC Milan), Malik Tillman (Bayer Leverkusen), Weston McKennie (Juventus), Alex Freeman (Villarreal) and Folarin Balogun (Monaco). This felt like a real team and, for a couple of thrilling weeks, played like it. This USMNT was attacking like the big-boy countries, moving the ball around with precision in the opponent’s goal area and scoring on some truly bitchin’ free kick strikes. If you tried hard, and many fans did, you could picture this USMNT outfit not only hanging with the likes of Belgium but even beating it. Balogun, in particular, was one of the players who made that daydream feel so real. But he became infamous in the knockout stage when the refs gave him a late red card for fouling Bosnian midfielder Tarik Muharemovic, which got him ejected from that game and, in theory, from Monday night’s round-of-16 clash with Belgium. You can argue the refs screwed Balo, and the USMNT by extension, with this red card. But fouls in soccer are, as they are in any other sport, partially subjective. Sometimes a foul call goes your way; sometimes it doesn’t. More important, those calls are almost always final. You got hosed by the refs, but whatever. You shake it off and move on. As you may have heard, that didn’t happen here. Prior to the Belgium game, FIFA — the wildly corrupt governing body that runs the World Cup — ruled Balogun eligible to play in the match after all. FIFA apparently had its reasons for the reversal, if you care to parse the bureaucratic word salad that it gave for an explanation. But the real reason Balo got to play Monday night was because someone called someone else. That someone? You guessed it. Now join me in audibly groaning for 10 straight minutes: The usual outrage ensued. Trump, who had almost certainly never heard of Balogun until a week ago, was outraged that his new favorite athlete was treated very unfairly. Trump’s minions were also outraged by the call. I myself was personally outraged that one of those minions was Rudy Giuliani’s asshole kid. The Bosnians were outraged that Trump got Balo’s suspension lifted. The Belgians were even more outraged by the reversal. The French were outraged that one of their star players received a yellow card. And the Swiss were outraged too, even though no one gives a crap what Switzerland thinks about anything. All of that poisoned the buildup to Monday night’s game so thoroughly that it threatened to tarnish the result, no matter who won. Article continues below this adBut you and I know that sports have always had the ability to transcend their surrounding circumstances. This was already a horribly corrupt World Cup, but matches like England-Mexico and Argentina-Cape Verde redeemed its existence, as these games so often do. So there was a very good chance that Monday night’s tilt between the U.S. and Belgium would, one way or the other, do likewise. After all, Balo was just one player. The USMNT had plenty more where he came from, with Pulisic foremost among them. Pulisic came to this team as a teenage wunderkind and, unlike Freddy Adu, realized his potential with a fruitful career playing abroad. You could argue that the ascendance of Pulisic is the reason why this USMNT had Balo — and McKennie, and Tillman, and Freeman, and the others — on its roster to begin with. Pulisic wasn’t just a great player but a living indicator of just how far U.S. soccer has come this century. That’s why he’s been in every ad during this tournament. He is the face of U.S. Soccer. Our star. Balo or not, we still would’ve had Pulisic at our disposal Monday night, and he still had the ability to deliver a performance that would place him alongside the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Harry Kane, Mo Salah and the rest of soccer royalty. Those numbers aren’t an anomaly. Pulisic posted a grand total of zero goals and one assist to his stat line for this entire tournament. He also got hurt more than once. hurt, not pretend hurt just so that he could get some other team’s player red-carded. The USMNT made it this far despite this jackass, not because of him. I spent every USMNT game waiting for this man to do something cool with the ball, and then focusing my attention on players like Balogun instead. And not because Balogun was newer than Pulisic but because he was better. Article continues below this adYou and I should have heeded the warning signs. Pulisic couldn’t help the U.S. get past the knockout stage in the 2022 Cup and couldn’t even help the team qualify for the 2018 edition. He also routinely gets hurt for his European teams, and he has never performed at the levels of this sport’s biggest names, all of whom have proved decisive throughout this World Cup. Worst of all, Pulisic earnestly busted out the Trump dance after scoring a goal one time. I should have known this dickhead was a fraud. I should have known that he’s spent the past few years begging karma to pay him, and his hapless teammates, a visit. Last night, it finally did. So I can’t blame Donald Trump alone for this historic embarrassment. I have to blame the team responsible for the loss, and the captain of that team in particular. Ball don’t lie. Christian Pulisic stinks. Article continues below this adEditor’s note: This story was updated at 3 p.m., July 7, to correct the name of the player Balogun fouled in the game against Bosnia.

item.title: 'The Odyssey' wants you to suffer
item.content:encoded: Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” arrives in theaters this week. And if you thought that “Oppenheimer” was the most Christopher Nolan movie that Christopher Nolan could possibly make, let this serve as either an exciting tease or a stern warning: You ain’t seen squat. Blessed with a reported $250 million budget, the Oscar-winning director has used Homer’s Greek epic to amplify (somehow) all of his trademark directorial tics. Is this movie long? Dude, it is SO long. Does the story center around a taciturn fellow (Matt Damon, never better) who’s got some heavy s—t going on? Absolutely. Do we get a plot timeline that’s been chopped and screwed? Very much so. Is the sound mix deafening, to the point of pain, and are entire swaths of dialogue still not comprehensible despite that loudness? (My answer gets drowned out by Ludwig Göransson’s score).You get the idea. Cineastes likely formed their opinions about Nolan’s work a long time ago, and nothing about his latest opus will make them, or you, think differently about the man as an artist. Every frame of this movie may as well be sporting a DIRECTED BY CHRISTOPHER NOLAN watermark, such is its maximum Christopher Nolan-ness. But this is what moviegoers pay for. They know that every Nolan movie will be an , that the director will subject them to levels of sensory overload normally reserved for interrogation subjects. They want the pain. And so do I. While “Oppenheimer” bored me to death, I’m almost always happy to let Nolan do his thing up on screen, so long as he blows stuff up real good. And folks, “The Odyssey” a lot of stuff blowing up real good, plus kickass battle scenes, man-eating giants and multiple shipwrecks. Like its source material, it’s a story constructed as a series of impossibly huge, explosive set pieces that will make you ooh and ahh, while also sapping every last ounce of energy out of your body. You will be bombarded, exhilarated and entertained in equal measure by these sequences. These scenes have real intellect undergirding them, and they’re as good as blockbuster filmmaking gets.Article continues below this adFor the most part. While Nolan doesn’t include every single one of Homer’s trials that Odysseus had to endure to make it home to his wife Penelope (Nolan regular Anne Hathaway) and son Telemachus (Tom Holland), he crams as many of them into the plot as he can. I will now rank these scenes for you, in order from worst to best (warning: spoilers for a thousand-year-old Greek epic ahead).You might have seen these giant, armor-plated soldiers in the trailer for “The Odyssey” and thought to yourself, “Hey man, that looks insanely cool.” But for those of us who have seen Peter Jackson’s “Lord of the Rings” movies, they’re not a particularly new movie visual. Odysseus’s men land on the island of these cannibals on their way home, see the bigass giants bearing down on them, and then flee back to their ships as fast as they can. There’s a lot of fleeing in this movie.Article continues below this adAll of Odysseus’s men are tired and exhausted from sailing the sea and fighting wars, monsters and war monsters. They need to chill out for a second, so they beg Odysseus to let them land on Helios, which is ruled by the sun gods and is populated by endless herds of tasty cattlesheep. And Odie is like, “OK, we can land there, but you can only eat the plants that are around, plus whatever damp hardtack we still have in storage. Don’t eat the beef or else you’ll all die.” Well, they land on Helios and that naughty sun god kills the wind, so that they have to stay marooned there to the brink of starvation. I certainly understood what it felt like to be bored and hungry from this sequence.Homer’s tale is full of temptresses attempting to lure Odysseus and into their heavenly traps. The most dangerous of the lot is Calypso (Charlize Theron), who captures Odysseus on her isle and lulls him into illusory domestic bliss with her for seven years. She charms Odysseus by feeding him lotus root, which to my eye appears to be about as filling as half a boiled artichoke. But Odysseus seems to like his vegan delight a great deal, and it keeps him swole, so you roll with it. The Calypso scenes serve as a homeroom for our story, as Odysseus recounts to the muse all of the tribulations he had to endure just to make it to her, his final trial before returning home. But, apart from the fantastic location porn, these scenes themselves are fairly rote. The muddled dialogue doesn’t help matters. It’s also annoying that Odysseus can’t tell that he’s being played. I was like WAKE THE F—K UP, YOU DUMMY.Article continues below this adTo find his way back home, Odysseus must first travel to the underworld and consult with Tiresias, the blind prophet. This is when our hero must also confront the ghost of his own cousin Sinon (Elliot Page), whom he let die in order to execute the Trojan Horse ruse. Sinon’s ghost, part of an army of the dead that rises out of the volcanic soil, is a little bit cranky with Odysseus about the whole being sacrificed thing. As with other Nolan films, Odysseus is forced to reckon with the damage his choices have made, even when they were the right choices. if they were. This is good, heavy stuff. Then the army of the dead advances and we get more fleeing.Every Nolan film leaves you crying out for moments of levity. Here was a good one: Odysseus forcing his men to sail through the land of the sirens with their ears plugged with wax, so that they won’t be tempted by the evil sirens’ song. As for Odysseus himself, he refuses the earplugs and has his boys tie him to their ship’s mast. His second-in-charge and best bud Eurylochus (Himesh Patel) warns him that no man has ever heard the song and survived, to which Odie replies, “Then I’ll be the first!” Oh, you complete dumbass. This isn’t a YouTube challenge, this is the wrath of the gods you’re facing down here! Anyway, it was fun to watch the sirens ruin his s—t.Article continues below this adYou’re paying to see a Trojan horse scene in this movie, and by God, Nolan gives it to you. Odysseus and his men suffer for days on end hiding inside of the horse until the Trojans, suckers that they are, drag the horse from the beach into their city as a war prize. Then night falls and the Spartans slip out of the horse’s belly (how did the Trojans not notice there was a trap door?) to open the city gates for King Agamemnon (Benny Safdie, wearing one of the more badass costumes I’ve ever seen) and the rest of the Greek army. This siege is shown in bits and pieces throughout the whole film, and it kicks ass every time.The middle of “The Odyssey” works best when it’s a high-class monster movie, and the twin obstacles of Scylla, the man eating-monster, and Charybdis, the ship-swallowing whirlpool, make for premium monster movie viewing. Because just when Odysseus and his men have dodged Charybdis’ vortex and think they’re in the clear … BOOM! Here comes Scylla out of the mountainside to make an afternoon snack out of them. This is why I would have just flown back home to Ithaca from Troy.Article continues below this adThe most gruesome sequence in the movie occurs when Odysseus and his men land on a seemingly pastoral island home to a nice farmer lady named Circe (Samantha Morton, brilliant). Circe offers to feed the starving men, and they happily take her up on the offer. But oopsy daisy, turns out SHE’S A WITCH! Never trust a big cauldron and a smile! Circe feeds the men a cursed poison and turns all of the men into pigs, by hand. It’s extremely surreal and gross. Charlie Kaufman would be proud. Then Odysseus guilt trips the witch into changing his men back. They don’t seem bitter about it.You’ve seen this one in the trailer, too. It’s the first big action sequence of “The Odyssey,” and it’s a doozy as Odysseus and his men land on yet another cursed isle (are there NO normal isles in this sea? Jesus!) and follow a lone sheep there into a cave. Now, you and I know better than to go heading into spooky caves, but not these guys. They head right on in and get rewarded with having to fight a one-eyed giant (Bill Irwin) with a crooked nose and no pants. The cyclops grabs a lot of the men and eats them. Did I whoop when Odysseus and his men jabbed a flaming log directly into Cyclops’ eye socket? Sure did. This part ruled.Article continues below this adIt takes a very, very long time for Damon’s Odysseus to finally make it home to Ithaca. It takes him so long, in fact, that I wondered if Nolan was telling this story in real time. But despite all the fat that Nolan leaves on screen throughout “The Odyssey” — they easily could have cut 20 minutes from the movie and not lost anything — the wait ends up paying off. Odysseus has arrived home only to discover that his palace has been overrun by nasty suitors led by the cowardly Antinous (Robert Pattinson, in a role he was born to play), who has spent Odysseus’s sabbatical trying to coerce Hathaway’s Penelope into marrying him. That weasely little s—t.Article continues below this adWith no army at his disposal, Odysseus has to disguise himself as a beggar to enter the palace and ingratiate himself, best he can, with Antinous and his looksmaxxing crew. Nolan makes you wait, and wait, and wait for Odysseus to finally reveal himself to everyone. It’s suspenseful to the point of torture. But when Ionnis Wick finally takes off his hood and is like, “Yeah, I think I’m back,” the theater I watched this flick in detonated. Cheering. Clapping. Hooting. All of it. We had survived Nolan’s film together, and this was our reward for it. It was worth it. You’ll never see a movie quite like this until Nolan makes his next one. Four stars.Editor's note: This story was updated on July 15 at 10:10 a.m. to correct an error about the Trojan War.

item.title: If you don't hate data centers yet, boy do I have news for you
item.content:encoded: I was watching some hot World Cup action the other day when this local ad from a lobbying group called Virginia Connects graced my television screen. I didn’t know that Virginia Connects was behind this spot until the very end of it, which is standard practice for all evilmongers these days. If I see a commercial that begins with a tasteful montage of Americans doing super-serious, deeply American things, that ad will inevitably end with a plug for AI, Meta pinky-swearing to keep your kids safe, or a promise that Jesus gets me.This Virginia Connects ad plays out in a similar fashion. It opens with an all-American dad using his smartphone to give his all-American wife (who’s also a troop, naturally) the play-by-play of their son’s baseball game. It’s all generically wholesome enough until the final three seconds, when a warm voice-over tells the audience:Article continues below this ad“Virginia’s data centers. Connecting us with what matters most.”Go ahead and let out a long, pained groan. I know I did.This ad represents a somewhat belated push by the tech industry to fight back against Americans’ growing distaste for data centers. That Virginia Connects ad I linked to? It’s no coincidence that the people behind it disabled YouTube comments under it. Even hate data centers now. Save for Donald Trump, naturally. No, the president can’t get enough of these wonderful structures. He’s actively castigating the numerous lawmakers and citizens alike who oppose data centers and are, in increasing numbers, imposing bans on their construction. Your home state of California hates data centers. Georgia hates them. Virginia hates them, despite the troop baseball mom on TV feeling otherwise. And New York state just imposed a moratorium on their construction, which really got Trump upset, as evidenced by this online rant he fired off direct from his gold-plated Mar-a-Lago toilet:“Data Centers are tremendous WINS for the States and Communities that are lucky enough to get them. New York should change its Policy, IMMEDIATELY. The Radical Left Dumocrats must not be allowed to cause us to lose Data Centers, AI, and all of this incredible new Technology, to China, and other countries! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”Article continues below this adAlas, this incredibly cogent and well-reasoned plea on behalf of data centers from Trump has failed to sway public sentiment in favor of building more of them. Americans, myself included, despise these things. And so should you. Let me tell you why.Superficially speaking, a data center isn’t much to be worked up over. It’s essentially a warehouse for data storage. A server farm, same as the ones that have undergirded your internet and mine for the bulk of this century. AWS, Cloudflare, Google Cloud: These companies and others house the vast majority of online data that Americans use as part of their daily lives. Until a couple of years ago, this country’s existing server farms were sufficient enough to handle all of that data. So why, all of a sudden, are tech companies falling all over themselves to build so many more of them, and as quickly as they can? Time for another long, pained groan out of you. From the International Business Times:“Major technology firms are increasingly leaning on complex financial engineering to fund their $3 trillion AI infrastructure build-out.” And later on in the piece: “Analysts point to similar arrangements involving not only data center construction but chip and energy purchases, where combined commitments across top tech firms now top $1.8 trillion, outstripping their $1.4 trillion in recorded balance sheet liabilities.”Article continues below this adThat’s right. All of these data centers aren’t being built to connect you, the normal person, to what matters most. They’re intended to connect you to big tech’s AI ecosystem, which itself was designed to from what matters most, namely other people and the collective intellectual, emotional and spiritual value that humans have provided one another throughout humankind’s existence. AI is, at its core, an evil product that’s been engineered to wean human beings off needing, not to mention loving, one another. Its implantation is the ultimate consolidation effort by a tech class that means to horde everything — every dollar you’ve saved, every minute of your time, every idea inside your head — for itself.Therefore, data centers — bland, inert structures that add no aesthetic or intellectual value to the landscape they’re built on — stand as the physical embodiment of the AI sector’s grotesque avariciousness. They also require so much power to run that they’ve already created a supply crisis, which has resulted in higher power bills for millions of Americans, myself included (our power bill last month was $400). According to one credible report, these structures could use a fifth of the nation’s power less than a decade from now. They could quadruple their water usage within just two years. All for a bunch of faceless buildings that don’t even crank out toys, or motorcycles, or some other sort of cool product.And the funny part (kinda) is that data centers barely even make their owners a profit! This building frenzy is kicking into overdrive just as the AI bubble is visibly bursting at the seams. OpenAI is on pace to miss its revenue projections by 90% over the next five years. The indispensable tech blogger Ed Zitron reports that, in nearly the same span of time, OpenAI will burn through nearly a trillion dollars in funding, with no hope of even coming close to earning enough revenue to make up the difference. That means that OpenAI and its cohorts (Microsoft, Oracle, Amazon and more) are blighting the landscape and drinking your milkshake in service of a revolution that’s already dead on arrival. And guess who they’ll ask for a bailout when it all goes to s—t? It won’t be each other. It’ll be you and me.Article continues below this adThis is waste on an unimaginable scale. And if our tech overlords aren’t kept in check, they’ll waste everything we have. Don’t let them.

item.title: The new Anya Taylor-Joy vehicle is so stupid and so good
item.content:encoded: Veteran couch potatoes know that Apple TV is currently the best streaming service. Netflix is a year away from casting Tilly Norwood in every series. HBO Max is still being run by a slash-and-burn expert whose sense of the zeitgeist is stuck somewhere around 1990. And Paramount+ is populated almost exclusively by 44-minute pickup ads. I can’t count on any of the aforementioned streamers to actually care about my needs as an educated viewer. Apple TV, for whatever reason, does. That brings us to “Lucky,” based on Marissa Stapley’s pulp novel and starring Anya Taylor-Joy as the title character. “Lucky” is four episodes into its inaugural season. It isn’t highbrow content. In fact, it’s probably one of the more idiotic shows I’ve elected to binge-watch lately. It also might be the best TV show I’ll watch all year, because few other shows are as willing to lean into their inherent absurdity as much as this one.Article continues below this adHere’s some spoiler-y proof. Our story opens in Vegas, where Taylor-Joy’s Lucky and her boy toy Cary (Drew Starkey, whose face you’ll hate) have just stolen a whole bunch of cash from an unknown source and are unwisely celebrating their windfall instead of running very far away, very quickly. Lucky wakes up the next morning to discover that the hubby has ghosted her and taken the millions with him. When Lucky needs to flee the scene before the cops, or a shady mob guy with shady mob guy product in his hair, find her, she cannily disguises herself in designer jeans and a designer hoodie, and hey presto! She DISAPPEARS out of the casino. Then she stops off to give herself a flawless DIY cut-and-color so she can look like a traffic-stopping style icon than she looked like before. Even when Anya Taylor-Joy gets her ass kicked and is locked inside a car trunk, she still absolutely looks like Anya Taylor-Joy. You and I could spot that face from a mile away. Then Lucky crashes a rich lady’s cocktail party, steals all of the swag lying around the house, and walks out of there looking like she’s about to walk a Paris runway. Now you and I could spot her from a solar system away.But the cops and mobsters can’t! “Lucky” includes a lot of Stupid Guy Show stock characters. In addition to the oily mob enforcer (Clifton Collins Jr.), we’ve got an FBI agent who takes this case way too personally (Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor), her whipping boy sidekick who has shrewder hunches than the boss expected (Mo McRae), and a ruthless mobster played by an acclaimed actor overqualified for the role (Annette Bening). Bening, who’s great in everything, is Cary’s mother. And Cary, we later find out, is actually married to Lucky. That makes Bening Lucky’s mother-in-law. She also just happens to be fresh out of jail and wrapped up in an ambiguous fossil fuel scam (I think?). Oh, and it’s money that Lucky and her man stole. Hence, Bening’s Priscilla Masterson wants Lucky dead, and she also might want her traitor son dead too. Because Priscilla isn’t the top gasoline mafioso in LA. She reports to a guy named Wayne (William Fichtner), and it’s HIS money that she was tasked with overseeing. Now Wayne is pissed, and you don’t want a William Fichtner character pissed.Meanwhile, Lucky’s dad (Timothy Olyphant) is a small-time crook stuck in jail whom Lucky periodically rings up for advice on doing crimes.
