item.title: Bluesky reply bot checker
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Automated reply bots on Twitter are a - as someone with a decent number of followers I attract a swarm of these, such that anything I post there attracts dozens of mindless automated replies.They've started manifesting on Bluesky as well.Unlike Twitter, Bluesky still has a freely available and useful API. The lack of such a thing doesn't slow down the bots, but it does make investigating them a lot more frustrating.So I had Opus 5.5 vibe code this tool, which examines any Bluesky profile for evidence of a likely reply bot.It looks for signals like replies posted within seconds of other posts from the same account, or accounts that never post their own content (or images or links) but instead consistently reply to messages from other, higher-follower users.It also looks for question marks, because I'm infuriated by reply bots that trick me into wasting my time answering a question that no human ever posed.

item.title: Combo Platter
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: Admit it, you were wondering where the hell the gas-station staples Combos came from just as much as I was. Anyway, I figured it out. At one point a drill was involved. As snack foods go, Combos I would describe as the perfect B-minus food. It’s a combination of crunchy and cheesy, nothing more, nothing less. They are the closest a road-tripper is going to get to chips and dip without stopping. But it’s not like the best food you’ve ever had. It’s the kind of thing that gets stuck in your teeth, and if you eat too many at once, it’s salty to the point of annoyance. But admit it: You’re in a gas station looking for sustenance, and it’s not like you walked into a Sheetz or a Wawa. Your options are limited, and as a result, you might just grab something you would never otherwise grab. You are the perfect customer for Combos, the snack food that didn’t reshape America, but instead is a reflection on your current circumstances. You are here. You need a bag of salty food. Combos is there, ready for you. Today’s Tedium answers the ever-lingering question about where Combos came from, why you can’t remember any of its commercials, and why that might actually be for the best. Drilling holes in pretzels: The forgotten Battle Creek company that eventually nailed CombosThere hasn’t exactly been many dedicated tomes written on the history of Combos, a food that isn’t the main entree on any normal person’s plate. It’s mass-manufactured snack food, and it’s been produced by one of the world’s largest food companies, Mars, since the late 1970s.But there was a time when it was thought to require a literal drill to produce. Yes, the signature hole that makes Combos unlike any food on grocery store shelves was originally produced with a drill. The overworked Dunkin’ guy says “time to make the donuts” as a camera crew catches his every move. The overworked Combos guy says “time to drill the pretzels,” as he takes a pretzel and cores it like a freaking apple.OK, I’m getting ahead of myself here, but I needed you to know about the drill thing, because it really just highlights how strange producing a food like Combos really is.The story of Combos starts with a pair of brothers, Richard and Walter Nelson. The brothers, based in Battle Creek, Michigan, were active entrepreneurs starting in the 1950s, when, with their father Walter Sr., they launched Wal-Rich Enterprises, which made toy guns, at Kellogg Field, a modern-day corporate airport that was used as a training base during World War II.By the 1970s, the brothers had shifted to contract work for various manufacturers, including General Motors and nearby Kellogg’s. But gradually, the brothers, now working under the Nelbros umbrella, started developing the patents for an unusual product: A pretzel filled with cheese. The first such patent filing, 1970s’s “Method of making a filled food item,” describes an attempt to solve the problem of putting a filling inside a fairly solid product, like a cracker:It is well-known practice to pierce a food item having a relatively open and porous interior, such as a cream puff or doughnut of pillow shape, and directly inject into such food item through the piercing member, a thick but flowable filling such as whipped cream, custard, fruit preserves, and jelly. The filling of hollow ice cream conetype items by various filling procedures, such as with soft ice creamlike material flowing from a faucet has also been proposed. Such procedures do not lend themselves to the filling of relatively solid items, and especially the solid and relatively brittle, sticklike, hard-crust items, and it was a recognition of the marketing possibilities of such items and a special method and apparatus for producing them, not commercially available, which led to the conception and development of the present invention.Accordingly, among the objects of the present invention is the provision of a new product in the form of an initially solid, relatively brittle, sticklike, crust-covered product which has been subsequently mechanically hollowed and filled with a suitable filler, and the method and apparatus for producing such product.Their solution to this problem they’ve found? Drill baby, drill:Another object of this invention is to provide an apparatus which will cut a bread stick to length, drill it substantially from the cut end to the other, fill same from the inside of said drilled opening, starting adjacent the bottom of same, with a suitable thick but extrudable filling material, and deliver same for further processing, using or packaging.If you’re a longtime reader of Tedium, you may know that this is kind of a wasteful process for producing a snack. The best snacks, such as cheese curls, come about because of happy accidents and byproducts. But this drilled-breadstick approach nonetheless was enough for Nelbros to launch this idea into a sellable product, which they, of course, called … shotzels.I’m not saying that it’s a bad name, but it certainly wasn’t good enough to win over the gas stations of the world. I was trying to figure out just how far idea of a cheese-filled pretzel shotzel reached beyond Battle Creek, and I found a lot of newspaper ads that suggest the company saw uptake for the product at a number of small delis around the country.How far did the shotzel get in Battle Creek? One of the few references I could find to shotzels in the city’s newspaper emerged around 1977 when it was promoted as one of the appetizers made available before a concert by the Battle Creek Symphony Orchestra. Combos may be low culture, but shotzels were apparently a hit with the city’s NPR crowd.Around this time, Nelbros was struggling with its factory situation, attempting to move facilities as it navigated a growing business. A 1978 article described a company in flux, along with a few others who were moving into a then-new industrial park.“It will take about six months to complete the building and get equipment in. We’re planning a 60,000-square-foot building that will accommodate a new 300-foot oven we have on order,” Richard Nelson told the newspaper. “We’ve outgrown our plant at Green and Jay streets and must relocate to expand.”Meanwhile, the brothers were continuing to develop the shotzel idea into something plainly recognizable to any modern snackhound. The strategy, as highlighted by a patent published in 1979: Get rid of the drilling.The objects of the invention are accomplished by apparatus and a method for making tubular food products wherein dough pieces in tubular shape are extruded onto supporting die members that hold the tubular dough piece during the time that it is raising and is being baked. Thereafter, the baked member is removed from the die member and is moved relative to a filling apparatus so that filler of a relatively softer food material can be deposited within the cavity formed in the baked tubular member. In one embodiment of the invention the supporting die members are transferred from separated conveyors for extruding, proofing, cooking and baking.Eseentially, rather than creating a single pretzel, filling it with cheese and cutting it up, this edition of the shotzel instead extrudes the bread onto tiny loops that already have holes in the middle, ensuring that they can easily be stuffed with cheese or some other kind of filling.Naturally, the candy manufacturing giant Mars got wind of this development, acquired it from Nelbros in 1979, gave it a name better than “shotzel,” and marketed it in gas stations nationwide. The rest is history.The number of current Combos flavors that the brand promotes on its website, a mixture of different breadings and different fillings. (Pretzel bread was first; the plainer cracker-style bread came half a decade later.) The brand also periodically sells some limited edition flavors, for folks who must eat Combos with sriracha flavoring or a faux-tortilla shell. As taste testing for this issue, I noshed a Garlic Parmesan flavor during a road trip, and, well, it felt like I was eating Combos.It’s so weird to me that there were no non-pretzel flavors of Combos for the first few years of its existence. Also, this ad screams “we don’t understand our target audience yet, so let’s aim super-broad.”The 2006 Combos marketing campaign that didn’t age particularly wellCombos are not really a product that needs advertising so much as distribution. They exist in a 7-Eleven. You pick them up instead of a bag of Bugles, and you’re on your way. Road trip commences.But that hasn’t stopped Mars from to market these things on television. The first such attempt came in 1982 in a format I’d call “Big Red”-core. It leaned heavily on the pretzel inspiration, rather than its bite-sized nature, which was really the selling point that mattered.But despite their lasting popularity, Combos have never been a favorite of advertisers. There’s not really a “Combos jingle” that people associate with the company. That meant that, when advertisers took steps to attempt to explain the appeal of Combos, they did so with the then-current language of hipness. This 1994 Combos ad, clearly riffing off of Bill Hicks and his close copycat Denis Leary, emphasizes the point. (At least it talks about the product!)Which meant that in the mid-2000s, when cable channels like Adult Swim and Spike TV were specifically targeting young men, Combos was something of an open canvas upon which big advertising firms could place their imprint.And given our cultural evolution since, it reads as particularly gnarly. The slogan says what they were going for: “What Your Mom Would Feed You If Your Mom Were A Man.”Basically, they got someone who looks very much like a man (played by E.J. Carroll, best known for a recurring role on the HBO show ), put him in a dress, and gave him some clearly adult sons. The visual effect comes off somewhat like John Carroll Lynch’s cross-dressing character in , without the ahead-of-its-time progressive elements that eventually (and unfortunately) led that story line to be dropped.The ads were designed for maximum absurdity (giving Combos to a sick son, saying grace over a bag of Combos), and to hit you with that in-your-face slogan right at the end. We’re a long way from handing these things out at the Battle Creek Symphony Orchestra.It was the brainchild of TBWA\Chiat\Day, the firm famed for much of Apple’s iconic advertising, most notably its then-recent “Get A Mac” campaign. And the campaign even won awards for its radio advertising.In an era when at least some have questioned whether late character actor Tim Curry’s career-making role in The Rocky Horror Picture Show is transphobic, even considering that film’s lasting relevance with the LGBTQ+ community, the ad hits a lot differently today. Less fodder, more extremely misguided attempt at making a gender-role joke.I get that some will probably defend this ad campaign, but it just feels like it would have worked just as well without putting E.J. Carroll in a dress. never had to pull the gender reversal to make effectively the same joke. And other media properties that did lean into cross-dressing, such as and , at least set up a framework for why the gender reversal was happening. The joke in this specific campaign was crass even then, but now it just feels gratuitous.You might be wondering, did Combos do better later on? Arguably, yes, though still attempting to present these gas station standbys in a way that appealed to the Slim Jims crowd. A 2012-era ad campaign, called “Bad Combos,” instead leaned into absurd “bad combination” situations. (This “witch doctor” variation is also fairly edgy.)Was this the right approach for Combos’ target audience of people who just got gas at a place they’ll never visit again? Who’s to say. But it’s telling that I can’t seem to find any recent examples of Combos ads that appeared on television. The Instagram account that gets updated a few times a year is probably enough.Honestly, they sell themselves—without the transphobic tropes.If Combos represents anything, it might be the sharp differences between how a creator perceives the product they developed, and how its acquirer approaches it.Currently, Combos are manufactured far from Battle Creek, Michigan, at a factory in Albany, Georgia. That’s right, friends. Combos are made in the U.S.A. The brand even sponsors a marathon in Albany, though admittedly I could not imagine eating Combos after a run. The salty flavor doesn’t exactly scream “runner-friendly food.”I understand why companies often feel compelled to lean into edgy marketing for the products they sell, but I secretly wonder if Combos would have been better off it it stuck to the marketing it had in the late ’80s and early ’90s. Nobody needed a version of Combos that tried to come off like Carl’s Jr. It is food you buy at a convenience store and don’t think about until the next time you’re on a road trip.(In some cases, you could argue that the marketing goes against how the founders would have perceived it. Fitting their Battle Creek roots, the Nelsons were devout Seventh Day Adventists, and Richard L. Nelson’s obit described him as a “prayer warrior.”)What if Combos, I don’t know, promoted its brand as the thing that its distribution network has long positioned it as? Nothing more, nothing less. It’s tasty, it’s portable. It sells itself. Nothing wrong with letting some other product have the “edgy” lane.Combos did not need edgy marketing to be awesome. I stand by that. Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal!Added a mention of Combo Man, Combos’ short-lived Marvel superhero persona. Thanks Marc Quill for calling it out!

item.title: rogue nation, moron president
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Donny Convict truly is the worst of us. he’s a burst trash bag of personality defects. can you think of something that wrong with him? there’s the preening vanity. imagine looking in the mirror, seeing that desiccated piss-mop perched atop your head, and going, ‘oh yeah, I’m really rocking it today.’then there’s the narcissistic grandiosity, and the overwhelming stupidity.he’s got fascist tendencies. he’s incapable of ever telling the truth, or admitting mistakes. he’s a cheater. he’s lazy and impulsive, with the attention span of a coked-up squirrel. he’s racist, transphobic, and misogynistic.he’s delusional, imagining that he’s entitled to all the power, all the money, and all the attention.it makes no sense for Donny reject Iran’s offer. think about it.imagine you’re the chief executive of a nation. imagine it’s mere weeks before an election that your party is sure to lose, because you’re fucked your country into a unpopular, unwinnable war that’s raised the price of everything. imagine that the country you’re warring with throws you a lifeline, and offers to restart negotiations.“I’m rejecting their deal. they want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately, because they’re losing so badly. you know. you don’t read that, or you don’t see that on the fake news. but we’re winning tremendously. we have total control of the— Hormuz Strait. massive amounts of oil are coming out of the Hormuz Strait. last night we had 29 ships come out. ummmm, they want to make deal, and I think that’s fine. I like making a deal, too. but uhhhhh, I’m not— that deal would not be acceptable. and what they want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait. you know why? because they’re dying. you know why they’re dying? they have no money coming in. ’cause they get their money from the Hormuz Strait.”every word that just seeped out of Donny’s rancid anus-mouth is either an outright lie, a contradiction of the previous sentence, or a big ball of — such as his boast that ‘29 ships’ passed through the Strait last night. “Live vessel trackers report ships currently underway in the Strait of Hormuz, which is about 2% of the normal prewar daily average of around 60 to 100+ ships.”look, agreeing to negotiate should be a no-brainer. Donny just had a win dropped right into his lap, and he’s too fucking dumb to realize it.do you know what would happen to the price of oil, if Dear Leader were to announce that he’s resumed talks with Iran? it would immediately plummet — five weeks before the midterms. think of the boon that would be for Republicans.but Donny won’t do that, because he has no ability to think strategically — and he’s a sadist who doesn’t care who his victims are, even if it’s his own party. he just truly gets off on being a dick.Republicans have to be tearing their hair out right now.boo fucking hoo, dumb-asses. the GOP should be thanking its lucky stars that Mitch McConnell isn’t alive to see any of this shit happening.The United States and the European Union on Friday rejected a declaration by member countries of the United Nations that pledged international collaboration and solidarity in preparing for and responding to pandemics.why reject this? for fuck’s sake, it was a purely symbolic gesture that wasn’t even legally binding. it would cost nothing to agree to it.The declaration, the product of a high-level U.N. meeting on pandemic preparedness, is largely ceremonial. It is not legally binding, and does not set rules for what countries should do during pandemics. But its universal endorsement would have signaled a powerful expression of global political commitment to the issue.have we all forgotten that the last global pandemic was only six years ago? no one was prepared for that shit, and look what happened. remember not being able to buy toilet paper? Donny — no doubt egged on by his whale-head-chainsawing lackey, the Marvelous Mister Measles — wants us to stick our heads back in the sand, so we can be just as unprepared for the pandemic. why? what does Donny even get out of it? is he just being a dick?oh wait — buried way down in the Times’ reported is the real reason for rejecting the declaration: The 2023 declaration, which the Biden administration supported, recognized “the need to tackle health inequities and inequalities, within and among countries.”Joe Biden was in favor of it, which automatically makes it Donny is such a fucking child.The Trump administration will move on Monday to sharply scale back fuel-efficiency rules for new cars and light trucks, gutting one of the government’s most significant efforts to reduce gasoline consumption and speed the country’s shift to electric vehicles.oh, come the fuck on — it’s the . remember when we used to be able to relax on the weekend? remember not hearing from the White House for 72 glorious hours? we don’t get weekends any more. the firehose of fuckery just sprays directly into our faces every second of every minute of every of every week of every month of the year.every single day these Donnyverse shitweasels wake up and go, ‘how can we fuck shit up today? whose mellow can we harsh? how about refusing to negotiate with Iran? or maybe rejecting a pandemic preparedness declaration? what if we gut clean air rules?’and then some asshole stands up and goes, ‘no, wait — I’ve got the best one yet! let’s put a baseball stadium in the middle of the pristine wilderness! oh my god, that shit would rule!’Major League Baseball has approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at a national park, officials from the White House and MLB confirmed Saturday.The administration has scouted locations in Grand Teton National Park to build a baseball park to host an MLB game, according to two other people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.it was bad enough that Donny built a human cockfighting ring on the White House’s south lawn, just so he could watch roided-out psychopaths beat each other to a bloody pulp. now he wants to build a baseball park in the middle of .oh, and you gotta love the way the Washington Post tries to sanewash the notion of fucking up the wilderness so that our sports-addicted president can get his rocks off.National parks are among the country’s most protected federal lands, and constructing a sports facility at Grand Teton could set a new precedent for the use of vast national park land in the Western United States.‘could set a new precedent’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that paragraph. we need to remember that our country is not Donny’s personal plaything. he doesn’t own the White House. he doesn’t own the Reflecting Pool — and he sure as shit doesn’t own our nation’s unspoiled wilderness. speaking of the Reflecting Pool, how about Donny finish what he started there, before bulldozing the Grand Tetons — because it sure as shit looks like Mister Ten-Second Attention Span has completely forgotten about it.if Dear Leader wants a baseball stadium, let him build one right on top of one of his vermin-infested golf motels.holy shit, that’s some prime nightmare fuel, right there.oh good, maybe that will shut Donny the fuck up for a whole day. maybe he and the Diaper Nurse will just quietly sit in the corner and canoodle, while happens all around them.maybe — — when I sit down at the laptop tomorrow morning to type out the day’s post, I’ll be able to say ‘huh, nothing happened on Sunday. here, enjoy some cat gifs.’I wouldn’t put any money on that happening, if I were you. mark my words, fuckery will inevitably be afoot today. you can set your watch to it — and lucky me, I’ll get to tell you all about it tomorrow.oh look — we’ve finally reached the bottom of the post, and it’s Daily Claudia time.here are a trio from the living room on Ms Spouse’s 66th birthday, February 7, 2016.have a great Sunday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Baty.net Editor
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: Usually, when I grow tired of editing blog posts using Markdown files in Emacs or whatever, I create a new blog using Ghost or something like it. This time, I did something different.Sometimes I just want a nice, easy, CMS for blogging. Emacs and a few lisp function are not that, so I asked Claude Code to make me a web app.At 7:00 am I sent the following to Claude:My blog at baty.net is managed locally using Eleventy. I would like to build a local web app that allows me to create new content. It should have "New Post", "New Journal", "New Page", and "New Note" options. The editor should handle Markdown, but it doesn't necessarily have to be "WYSIWYG" . There's should be a way to start the local server ("just serve") and deploy ("just deploy"). The blog is currently in ~/sites/baty.net.I walked away and made breakfast.At 7:27 am Claude said this:I used it to write a test post, and it worked, first try. The app needed no edits. I later added a few niceties, but all-in this first version took less than an hour to build and I'm using it to write this post.

item.title: Sunday Weird History Lesson: The Man Who Declared War on the Moon
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There is something wonderfully absurd about the idea of declaring war on the Moon.It isn’t a country. It doesn’t have a government. It doesn’t have an army. It doesn’t even belong to anyone.At least, that’s what most people would assume.Dennis Hope had a different idea.In the 1980s, Hope, an American entrepreneur from Nevada, discovered what he believed was a loophole in international law that allowed him to claim ownership of extraterrestrial real estate. He eventually began selling plots of land on the Moon to customers around the world.He didn’t literally declare war on the Moon, despite the colorful way the story is sometimes told. His real claim was considerably stranger: And he wasn’t stopping with the Moon.Hope also claimed large portions of Mars, Venus and Mercury, turning himself into one of the most unusual property entrepreneurs of the modern era.The story is part legal experiment, part business venture, part publicity stunt—and entirely bizarre.The Moon Needs a LandlordDennis Hope’s story began with a personal financial problem.According to accounts of his business, Hope was going through a difficult period in his life in the late 1970s and early 1980s. He began thinking about ways to make money and eventually became interested in an obscure area of international law.The answer seemed obvious.The United States had landed astronauts there. The Soviet Union had sent spacecraft. Other countries had photographed it, studied it and sent probes toward it.But no country had officially claimed the Moon as its own.Hope started examining the legal agreements governing outer space and noticed language concerning national governments claiming territory in space.His interpretation was that these restrictions applied to nations, not necessarily private individuals.That was the opening he was looking for.The central document in Hope’s argument was the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.The treaty established the principle that celestial bodies such as the Moon should not become the territory of individual nations.Governments could not simply plant a flag on the Moon and declare:“Congratulations, everyone. We own this now.”The treaty also established that outer space and celestial bodies were to be used for peaceful purposes and that they were not subject to national appropriation.Hope interpreted this differently.He argued that while governments were prohibited from claiming celestial territory, the treaty did not explicitly prevent an individual from doing so.So he filed paperwork claiming ownership.The logic was unconventional.The consequences were even more unconventional.Or at least, he believed he did.Selling Lunar Real EstateHaving claimed the Moon, Hope faced a practical question.What do you do with a Moon?His answer was surprisingly capitalist.Hope established the Lunar Embassy, a business that marketed lunar property to customers.People could purchase certificates claiming ownership of plots of land on the Moon.Depending on the package, buyers could receive maps, certificates and other documentation identifying their supposed lunar property.Suddenly, ordinary people could become extraterrestrial landowners.A person who couldn’t afford a house on Earth could theoretically own several acres on the Moon.The idea was irresistible.It combined the novelty of space exploration with the familiar language of real estate.Instead of buying a vacation property in Florida, you could buy property overlooking a lunar crater.There was just one minor problem.The World’s Most Inaccessible Real EstateBuying land is generally considered more useful when you can actually visit it.Moon property had an obvious disadvantage.There were no utility connections.There wasn’t even a reliable way to send a moving truck.A lunar homeowner couldn’t call a contractor and say, “I’d like a two-bedroom house built next Saturday.”Even today, decades after Hope began selling lunar property, private citizens cannot simply travel to the Moon and inspect their real estate.That didn’t stop people from buying.The novelty was the point.A lunar property certificate made for a memorable gift, conversation piece or novelty purchase.It was less like buying a suburban backyard and more like buying a tiny piece of humanity’s future.Millions of Lunar HomeownersHope’s business attracted customers from around the world.According to claims associated with the Lunar Embassy, millions of people have purchased extraterrestrial property through the company.Whether those buyers actually obtained legally enforceable property rights is a completely different question.The certificates certainly gave customers something tangible.They could hold a document saying that they owned a particular parcel of the Moon.But possessing a certificate isn’t necessarily the same thing as possessing a legally recognized property title.That distinction becomes extremely important when dealing with real estate located approximately 240,000 miles away.Can Anyone Actually Own the Moon?This is where the story gets complicated.The Outer Space Treaty is widely regarded as establishing that nations cannot claim sovereignty over celestial bodies.But private property rights in space are a much more complicated subject.Hope’s interpretation has never become an internationally recognized system of lunar property ownership.There is no global government that has officially recognized his claim.No major space agency treats his property maps as authoritative.And there is no lunar land registry accepting applications for backyard swimming pools.In practical terms, buying one of Hope’s certificates doesn’t give someone an internationally recognized piece of lunar territory in the same way that buying a house on Earth gives you legally enforceable property rights.That hasn’t stopped the business from continuing.The Moon Doesn’t Send LawyersOne reason the scheme is so entertaining is that it exposes the enormous gap between legal theory and physical reality.Imagine trying to enforce your lunar property rights.Someone lands on your property.And suppose the person refuses to leave.You have a trespasser on the Moon.The problem becomes even more complicated because there is no universally accepted lunar government capable of enforcing ordinary property law.Earth has spent thousands of years developing systems for buying, selling, taxing and defending land.The Moon doesn’t have any of that.The Business Became a Cultural PhenomenonRegardless of the legal arguments, Hope understood something important about human psychology.People love the idea of owning something extraordinary.Space has always had enormous cultural appeal.The Apollo missions transformed the Moon from a distant object in the night sky into a place humans could actually visit.Hope took that fascination and turned it into a commercial product.For a relatively small amount of money, a customer could tell friends:“I own land on the Moon.”That sentence alone was worth something.It was a great conversation starter.It was an unusual birthday present.It was a piece of space-age memorabilia.And for some customers, it may have represented something more philosophical—a symbolic connection to humanity’s future beyond Earth.Hope Didn’t Stop With the MoonHope expanded his extraterrestrial real estate empire to other planets.He claimed large portions of Mars, Mercury and Venus.He also sold property packages associated with these worlds.The idea became increasingly surreal.A customer could potentially own a piece of the Moon, Mars or another celestial body without ever leaving Earth.In a way, Hope created the world’s most speculative real estate market.There were no open houses.No photographs of the kitchen.No school district ratings.No neighborhood association.And absolutely no chance of driving by to see whether the previous owner had left junk in the garage.The strangest question is whether these purchases could ever become useful.Imagine that lunar settlements become common in the future.Suppose humans eventually establish permanent cities on the Moon.What happens to Hope’s customers?Could someone show up at a lunar settlement with a decades-old certificate and say:That’s where the uncertainty becomes enormous.Future governments and international organizations would have to determine how lunar resources and territory are governed.They may create entirely new systems for habitation, scientific research, mining and settlement.There is no guarantee that a certificate purchased from a private company today would have any legal standing under those future systems.In other words, lunar property buyers are betting on a legal future that hasn’t been written yet.So how did a man selling Moon real estate become associated with the idea of declaring war on the Moon?The answer is mostly storytelling.Hope didn’t actually assemble an army.He didn’t send tanks toward the Sea of Tranquility.He didn’t fire missiles at the lunar surface.He didn’t stand outside a government building and announce hostilities against Earth’s satellite.His real achievement was considerably stranger.He looked at a celestial body that humanity had admired for thousands of years and asked:That’s what makes the story so memorable.The Ultimate Real Estate PitchDennis Hope’s lunar property scheme sits somewhere between entrepreneurship, legal interpretation and science-fiction fantasy.Critics can argue that his interpretation of international space law doesn’t establish genuine ownership.They can point out that no internationally recognized authority has validated his lunar real estate claims.They can laugh at the idea of selling land that nobody can currently visit.All of those objections are reasonable.But Hope still accomplished something remarkable.He turned an abstract legal question into a business.He took something that had always seemed completely outside the real estate market—the Moon—and gave it addresses, maps, certificates and customers.He transformed lunar land into a product.The story of Dennis Hope is ultimately less about whether someone actually owns the Moon and more about the extraordinary things people will buy when imagination, technology and commerce collide.Human beings have always wanted to own unusual things.People collect meteorites.They buy pieces of historic buildings.They purchase celebrity memorabilia.Hope simply took the idea one enormous step further.He offered people the chance to own a piece of another world.Maybe the certificates will someday become valuable historical curiosities.Maybe future lunar governments will completely ignore them.Maybe humanity will eventually build cities on the Moon and discover that the entire concept of extraterrestrial real estate needs to be reinvented.Or maybe lunar property will remain exactly what it is today: a fascinating novelty that allows someone to look up at the night sky and say, with a straight face:Dennis Hope never actually declared war on the Moon.He did something much stranger.

item.title: Kākāpō Party
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: For my closing slide I wanted to celebrate, and I had seen some buzz around how good Claude Opus 5.5 was at creating pixel art animations. So I rounded up three Kakapo photos from Google image search and dropped them into Claude with this prompt:Here are some photos of kakapo parrots just to remind you what they look likeI need you to make an animation in animated pixel art on HTML 5 canvas of obviously pixel art kakapo jumping up and down having a party with confetti and suchlike - there should be at least 20 of themI wanted to embed it in a Keynote presentation file, so I downloaded the HTML and told a local Claude Code session:Make me a video of file:///Users/simon/Downloads/kakapo-party.html - you need to load it in a browser and click on it a few times to get the confetti effect, the video should be 15s longdon't start clicking until 3s inmake sure several clicks are spread around the clickable areaClaude Code used Playwright (transcript here) and produced this video, which was exactly what I needed for my final slide:Here's the full Playwright script it used, which was pleasingly short:., , [ (, , ), (, , ), (, , ), (, , ), (, , ), (, , ), (, , ), (, , ), (, , ), (, , ), ] () : ..() .({:,:}, , {:,:}) .() .() .() ,,: .((, (.()))) ..(,) .((, (.()))) .(); .()

item.title: this week in stupid: September 26 edition
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: as another stupid week comes to a close here in America, let’s look back at the dumbest fucking shit that happened.monday: fly the furry skies“many — listen to this — many airline pilots, flight attendants, and air traffic controllers are part of the furry community. lord help us. it’s terrifying, when you think about it.”furries. Tuberville is talking about , the subculture of people who get off on dressing up as animals. according to our hallucinating senator here, there’s an epidemic of cats and dogs piloting aircraft. look, I fly often. I’ve never seen a flight crew dressed up as , have you? of course you haven’t — and neither has Senator You Should Have Worn Your Fucking Helmet, Asshole. but this imaginary issue is what Tommy wants us to be focused on — as if we don’t have enough problems on our plates already.after getting roundly mocked by the entire world for his dumbfuckery, Terminally-Concussed Tommy did what all dipshits do — he doubled down on the dumbfuck.I know the deranged Democrats don’t like the fact that I called out the insane FURRY CULTURE this week. But the truth is, there is an ALARMING number of these DERANGED people working in our airline industry. Don’t believe me? Just a few months ago, PILOTS were MEOWING and BARKING at each other over the radio at DCA.oh my god, these pilots were MEOWING and BARKING. the horror! The audio of pilots meowing and barking at DCA was a longstanding aviation joke/meme on the emergency guard frequency 121.5, unrelated to furries or any subculture, per reports and pilot accounts.. it’s a thing pilots and controllers do to blow off steam, because their jobs are stressful as fuck. this whole ludicrous episode is Peak MAGA. they misunderstand a joke, get all worked up over it for nothing, and then waste everyone’s time by actually standing up in the well of the Senate and expecting us to run around with our hair on fire over bullshit.are there any actual furry pilots? I don’t know. I don’t care. who gives a fuck? all that matters is that we go up in the air, and we come back down safely. beyond that, I don’t give a shit how anyone is dressed, as long as they do their job.no one gives cares, Tuberville. we want healthcare. we want gas that doesn’t cost an arm and a leg. fix that shit. then we can worry about your imaginary problems.maybe our terminally-concussed senator here shouldn’t be flying without a helmet.tuesday: let them eat now here’s Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins with an important message for the American consumer: don’t bother her with your problems. .“if [beef] is too expensive … you can eat chicken, salmon, eggs — there are other great sources of really good protein.”but now that Dear Leader has clownfucked our once-strong economy straight into the shitter, by imposing incoherent tariffs and blundering into an unwinnable don’t-you-dare-call-it-a-war on Iran, the message from the Donnyverse is now go find something else to eat, fuckface.wednesday: try growing a personality, bro “the thing that people miss in modernism, that we take for granted, we have normalcy bias in a certain direction. we consider normal what is actually insane. we consider normal women having unsupervised access to one another — all the time. we consider normal women — like all these things. women having political rule. we consider normal women living unattached from a male, like a husband, like a father, then a husband, for lengthy periods of time. we consider normal — you could fill in the blank with all of these modern feminist outworkings of the original feminist vision.”holy fuck — that’s a lot of words, just to say ‘I’ve never known the touch of a woman.’grow a personality, bro. stop being such a whiny little boy. if you treat women like people, instead of imagining that they’re some subservient species that owes you their attention, you’ll do fine. trust me.thursday: Peak Stupid just got out-peaked “Xi JinPing refused to put his hand over his heart during the US National Anthem just now.”oh my god. the stupid on Laura’s post is about ten feet thick. how can we possibly dig our way out of it?Yes. Because he’s not American.that’s right, President Xi did exactly what he was supposed to do — — because he’s not an American.which brings us quite smoothly to—friday: the further adventures of Some Fucking Idiot™Friday was Day Two of some fucking idiot’s playdate with his despot inamorato, President Xi of China.Trump in 2011: The president of China came a few months ago and we gave him a state dinner. Now, when people are screwing you, you don't give them state dinners.Trump in 2015: I would not be throwing Xi Jinping a dinner. I would get him a McDonald’s hamburger and say ‘we have to get down to work.’ We’re giving him a state dinner and what he has done is sucked all of our jobs.holy shit. how embarrassing.Melania trying to free her hand from Trump's grasp is sad to watch. you can imagine her going, ‘fock you, Donal, I no care eef you fall. maybe diaper norse want to hold you hand.’that shit must be giffed for posterity’s sake.NEW ANGLE: 📸Melania appeared to be giving Donald a piece of her mind after he held her hand not once but twice. 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Trump points toward the media, pauses then becomes animated. Imagine if the beast had media coverage 🤣🤣you sure hate to see such a formerly happy couple going through a bad patch, don’t you?Now that the pool is there, Trump is finally getting questions: “Did you call on President XI to stop buying oil from Iran? Why are you banning media outlets? Should taxpayers pay for ads about you”but even though the press was actually asking some important questions for a change, not one reporter stood up to ask the one question America wants an answer to, ‘what the fuck is wrong with you?’how fucking idiotic was that?and now, let’s put a close to This Week in Stupid and have us some Daily Claudia.today’s let’s have us some random beachy fun. here’s Ms Spouse with some ocean-side dining, from August 24, 2002.here’s Katie and her mom in Newport, Rhode Island, early 1990s.and this last one’s from Plymouth, MA, early 1990s.have a non-stupid Saturday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future:practice self-care. do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Parametrised tests in Rust with named parameters
item.author: Alex Chan
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been revisiting some of my small Rust utilities this week, and I wanted to improve the test suite. There’s a lot of repetition, and I wanted to switch to parametrised tests, a pattern I use a lot in Python and Go. (These are also called “table-driven tests”.)Parameterised tests allow you to write the test logic once, then run it with many different inputs and expected results. This reduces repetition, highlights variation, and simplifies adding new cases.For example, in my thumbnail creator, I want to create a thumbnail with various image formats, and check the thumbnail has the correct filename and dimensions. Rather than copy-pasting test functions, I wanted to declare test cases with named fields, like this: img_path target TargetDimensionMaxWidth expected_filename expected_dimsSupporting this syntax required me to create a custom Rust macro.I found three existing approaches to writing this type of test in Rust:Use a loop over the test cases. This is the simplest approach: define our test cases in an array, then iterate over them one-by-one.#[test] test_cases fibonacciinput expectedThis is easy to write and understand, but Rust’s standard assertions don’t give us test case isolation. If one case fails, the test stops immediately and skips the rest.(Go’s testing library has , which marks a test as failed but allows it to continue running. When a test fails, you often have more information than if the test had failed immediately. I now miss this when working in other languages.)Define a macro with positional arguments. Many guides, such as over-code’s article, define custom macros with positional arguments.fib_testNamed test cases are nice, but positional arguments hurt readability if you have more than a few parameters.
#[rstest] #[case(1, 1)] #[case(6, 8)] #[case(10, 55)] #[case] #[case] expected fibonacciinputIf I was working in a larger codebase, I’d compare these libraries and pick my favourite.I deliberately skipped them this time, because I only use Rust for tiny personal tools, and I write it as a learning exercise. I’d rather write a basic version myself and learn something new, than use somebody else’s library and miss out on the lesson.Since I couldn’t find a macro that gave me named parameters, I decided to write my own.Here’s the complete macro invocation for my image thumbnailer, with three test cases:image_thumbnail_tests img_path target TargetDimensionMaxWidth expected_filename expected_dims img_path target TargetDimensionMaxWidth expected_filename expected_dims img_path target TargetDimensionMaxWidth expected_filename expected_dimsThe goal is to have clear, self-documented test cases. You can see what the test does and how to add a new test case without reading the body of the macro.Here’s the macro definition, with extra whitespace to make the structure more obvious: $( ident img_pathexpr targetexpr expected_filenameexpr expected_dimsexpr $( #[test] PathBuffrom$img_path test_dir create_thumbnailpathout_dir $targetunwrapthumbnail_path out_dirjoin$expected_filenamethumbnail_pathexistsget_dimensionsthumbnail_path $expected_dimsIf we zoom out, the structure of a declarative macro looks like a match expression:I think of the two halves are input/output, but they’re really called matcher/transcriber:The left-hand side (). The matcher defines a pattern of Rust tokens the input code must match precisely, including commas and brackets (but ignoring whitespace). works like a regular expression, matching zero or more instances of the enclosed pattern. and match a Rust identifier and expression, respectively, and bind them to metavariables (similar to named capture groups in regexes).I deliberately designed my pattern to resemble Rust’s struct syntax. Macro inputs don’t have to be valid Rust code, but I wanted something that would look familiar in a Rust file.The right-hand side (). The transcriber is a template for Rust code, which gets substituted in at compile time, replacing metavariables with values captured by the matcher.Here, the iterates over the matches and creates a corresponding function with a attribute. This attribute is why we need to use a macro – there’s no way to dynamically generate new test functions in Rust without macros.When compiled, the macro gets replaced with all the generated code from the transcriber, as if I’d written out the individual tests in full:#[test] PathBuffrom test_dir create_thumbnailpathout_dir TargetDimensionMaxWidthunwrapthumbnail_path out_dirjointhumbnail_pathexistsget_dimensionsthumbnail_path
#[test] PathBuffromThis means all of my test cases run as separate tests, so I get all the benefits of individual test functions without having to copy-paste lots of boilerplate throughout my codebase.I’ve seen custom macros pop up in the few Rust codebases I’ve read, and it feels good to have a better understanding of how they work. I used to copy-paste the same snippets thoughtlessly from project to project, but now I know what the different brackets and asterisks mean. The next time I write a macro or read somebody else’s, I’ll know what’s going on.
